summary: The chapel at Council Road Baptist Church in Oklahoma City turned into a science lab on Oct. 5-6. Microscopes, beakers and test tubes weren’t in the room, but this Sending Church Lab drew nearly 40 people representing 12 Oklahoma Baptist churches committed to send and care for international missionaries well. The Sending Church Lab, facilitated by the International Mission Board, brought pastors, church leaders and missionaries together for two days of discussion, self-assessment and planning ce
content: Staff members at First Baptist Church in Wagoner, Oklahoma, evaluate their church’s involvement with missions and missionary support. IMB Photo The chapel at Council Road Baptist Church in Oklahoma City turned into a science lab on Oct. 5-6. Microscopes, beakers and test tubes weren’t in the room, but this Sending Church Lab drew nearly 40 people representing 12 Oklahoma Baptist churches committed to send and care for international missionaries well. The Sending Church Lab, facilitated by the International Mission Board, brought pastors, church leaders and missionaries together for two days of discussion, self-assessment and planning centered on one question: What does it mean for a church to truly be a sending church? For Mike Wall, a global missions ministry partner of Oklahoma Baptists, the answer begins with churches reclaiming responsibility for the Great Commission. Wall first attended a Sending Church Lab last year in Tulsa with few expectations. He left convinced more churches needed the training. “When I went there, I thought, ‘You’ve got to do this in Oklahoma City,’” Wall said, “because of the content and how much our churches need something just like this.” After observing churches work through the exercises in the lab, Wall said he was encouraged by an emphasis on local church ownership in missions. “We can’t just send our people and say, ‘OK, now this is your job, IMB,’” he said. “We have to do our job in sending, preparing and training the best ‘sent ones’ so that when they get to the field, they can already hit the ground running.” Bryan Wooten, IMB senior church engagement specialist, leads a Sending Church Lab at Council Road Baptist Church in Oklahoma City. He is emphasizing the importance of sending churches assessing and equipping future IMB missionaries. IMB Photo Leading the lab was Bryan Wooten, IMB senior church engagement strategist, who developed the concept after seeing the need for stronger relationships between missionaries and local churches. “A Sending Church Lab is our attempt to raise up a host of IMB sending churches,” Wooten said, crediting the North American Mission Board for doing similar events and having successful results. The lab helps churches understand what Wooten calls the church engagement pathway: praying, cooperating, partnering and sending. While many churches faithfully pray, give and go, he said sending requires something more intentional. “Sending includes taking responsibility for an IMB missionary by providing ongoing encouragement, accountability and soul care throughout their term of service,” he explained. During the two-day event, participants gathered around whiteboards to evaluate their church’s missions practices, identify strengths and weaknesses and develop plans for improvement. “We don’t just need to deliver content,” Wooten said. “We need to invite churches to do some work on their own.” Rather than simply listening to presentations, attendees worked through practical questions about prayer, giving, short-term missions, missionary assessment and long-term care. Wooten said churches consistently tell him the greatest benefit is clarity. “They are thankful for clarity on what an IMB sending church is and what our roles and responsibilities are,” he said. For IMB missionaries Peter and Katie Weeks, that clarity is especially valuable. They participated in the lab alongside church leaders. Their real names have been changed to protect their work in Southeast Asia. “There’s no other place I’d rather be during these few days than here,” Peter said. Katie appreciated the interactive nature of the training. “I really appreciate the way they’re actually requiring information from the different churches and encouraging dialogue about how they can go through the steps,” she said. From a missionary perspective, she believes the lab addresses a common challenge. “It’s hard to know sometimes as churches how to be a good sending church and how to support missionaries,” she sa

content: It’s feasting season. Thanksgiving. Advent. New Year’s. But for Americans in particular, is there such a thing as a non -feasting season? Our society has a bizarre love-hate relationship with food, pulling the plate toward us with one hand while pushing it away with the other. On the one hand, about 40 percent of adults are clinically obese; on the other, more than one in eight adults rely on GLP-1 to suppress their appetite. We want food and we want to want food less. We struggle to break free from the clutches of Big Food, so we look to Big Pharma for help. Happy Thanksgiving? What’s the remedy for this gastronomic schizophrenia? As counterintuitive as it sounds, godly feasting provides an antidote to foolish gluttony. Feasting vs. Feeding The Bible has a lot to say about food, not just in isolated verses but in plot points central to the arc of Scripture. Many of the most egregious sins centered on food. For instance, the first sin involved rebellious eating, looking to something forbidden in search of goodness (Genesis 3:6). After the exodus, Israel grumbled about their desire for Pharaoh’s pots of meat (Exodus 16:3). Then, when the Lord provided manna in the wilderness, Israel reenacted the sin of Eve when they gathered food on the Sabbath against God’s command (Exodus 16:27–30). But the Bible also commends feasting, both spiritual and physical. Jesus offers himself as the bread of life, given for the nourishment of the saints in exile (John 6:35). And the church looks forward to a meal at the consummation of history, the marriage feast of the Lamb (Revelation 19:9). Between the resurrection and return of the Lamb, we weekly feast on his body and blood, anchoring our minds on what Christ has done and what Christ will do (1 Corinthians 11:23–26). Godly feasting leans into our place in between the times by remembering with gratitude what was and anticipating with joy what will be. All the blessed feasts in the Scriptures are communal celebrations . Something extraordinary has happened; raise a glass to the King! We shouldn’t eat what we regularly eat today; instead, “bring the fattened calf and kill it, and let us eat and celebrate. For this my son was dead, and is alive again; he was lost, and is found!” (Luke 15:23–24). We break from feeding ourselves (simply giving our body what it needs) in order to feast (eating and drinking more than we need) as a blessed means of joyously celebrating the work of God in history. But most Christians rarely, if ever, truly feast with mindful gratitude. We just overeat. Spiritual Malnutrition “A companion of gluttons shames his father” (Proverbs 28:7). The glutton does not feast; his god is his belly. He looks for deliverance in his next snack, his next meal, his next drink. He does not fully grasp that man does not live by bread alone. He is not marked by gratitude. The emptiness in his soul, the purposelessness of his life, and the joylessness of his ease have taken root as a spiritual disease. “A glutton is one who raids the icebox for a cure for spiritual malnutrition,” Frederick Buechner observed ( Wishful Thinking , 35). Americans, overall, remain locked in a permanent state of pseudo-feasting. Our culture combines industrial-grade, highly addictive food products and dopamine-seeking, nihilistic joylessness. We mindlessly munch. Often, we hardly even taste or enjoy our food. (A 2026 JAMA study revealed 69 percent of kids and 78 percent of adults use screens while eating.) This is an often-undiscussed problem within the church. I don’t know any Christians who intend to be gluttonous. But I know many, myself included, who have at times felt buried by the shame that follows an episode or season marked by a lack of self-control. We know we cannot make peace with sin, but we aren’t sure what this specific path of repentance looks like. So, when believers recognize the shameful pattern, we try to restrict our calories or go on a diet, which doesn’t stick. We purge and we binge — godless,

title: Are My Prayers Selfish?
summary: How do we know if we’re praying according to God’s will? Pastor John distinguishes unfaithful, selfish prayer from God-honoring, faithful prayer. Listen Now
content: Audio Transcript If we transcribed our prayers from the last year and shared them with each other, what would be obvious? Would it show lofty prayers for the nations? Would we be found praying most often that God’s name be hallowed on earth? Or would we see in those transcripts a lot of self-centered prayers that constantly revolve around our daily needs? And if that was what we found, would that really be a problem? As we will read in our Bible reading, 1 John 5 tells us that if we ask for anything according to God’s will, he will hear us. Today on Ask Pastor John: Are my prayers too selfish? It’s the question on the mind of Bridget. She’s a college student at UMass Amherst. “Pastor John, hello, and thank you for the Ask Pastor John podcast. I’ve been thinking a lot about this question of prayer. In 1 John 5:14–15,” in our reading tomorrow, “we receive the great promise that if we ask for anything according to God’s will, he hears and answers us. First Peter 5:7 welcomes us to cast all our cares on him. But then James 4:3 warns us that prayers driven by selfish motives won’t be answered. “I’m trying to fit these texts together in practice. We are encouraged to bring all our cares to God, so I get confused about how much we need to pre-align them with his will before we even speak them. Are we truly free to pray for anything, or are we only supposed to pray for certain cares? What I’m really trying to figure out is this: before I start praying for something specific I really want, how can I know if my desire is in line with God’s will or if the desire is selfish?” The Danger of Selfish Prayer Maybe digging into the context of James 4:3, which Bridget refers to, might shed light on how to know if our motivations are pleasing to God when we come to him in prayer. It’s surprising, even shocking imagery that we find here in James 4:1–5. Listen: “You do not have, because you do not ask. You ask and do not receive, because you ask wrongly.” Now, that’s the question: What’s “wrongly”? What is it to pray badly? “To spend it on your passions. You [adulteresses]!” Now, the translation “adulteresses” is important. It is plain, straightforward, and feminine (moichalides). To translate it “adulterous people” doesn’t help us. It is feminine, and it is “adulteresses,” and the image being created is crucial, and you can’t see it without the word adulteresses: “You adulteresses.” There are people in this church who are acting like adulteresses. They are acting like they belong to God as their husband while they’re acting like an unfaithful wife. “Do you not know that friendship with the world is enmity with God?” That is, a wife who goes after other lovers (namely, the world) is going to make her husband angry — justifiably jealous (namely, God). “Therefore whoever wishes to be a friend of the world,” the paramour down the hall, “makes himself an enemy of God,” the jilted husband. “Or do you suppose it is to no purpose that the Scripture says, ‘He yearns jealously over the spirit that he has made to dwell in us’?” That’s what a good husband does. A good husband feels indignant and has a deep sense of, “You’re mine. You shouldn’t give yourself to another man.” “Selfishness is when you want something and you’re going to seek it whether it dishonors God or not.” So, we’re talking about prayer. We’re talking about prayer in this paragraph. And James is saying there is a kind of prayer that treats God like a cuckold. It refers to a husband whose wife is cheating on him. That’s a cuckold. Christians are making God into a cuckold. How? When it says they are praying just to spend it on their passions. The picture is of an unfaithful wife who asked her husband for $50 so she can go down the hall and pay another man to have sex with her. That’s the picture. She’s using prayer to cheat on her husband, God. What Is a Selfish Prayer? How does that help us answer the question of how to sort out whether we are praying in accord with God’s will or being selfi

content: “Hold the lettuce.” The simple sentence, perhaps stated more frequently than we might hope, captures a crucial hallmark that predominates in the thinking of many. At a recent lunch with a friend, I saw this firsthand. For my friend, it wasn’t just the lettuce. The instructions he gave restrained the cook from adding anything remotely vegetable-like to the hamburger. Notwithstanding my jibe, my friend held fast to his decision. He was the one ordering. And he expected (rightly so!) to be served what he desired. After all, the customer is king. This cluster of expectations animates the modern marketplace. We want products tailored to our specific needs. We seek out services that let us pay only for what we want. We get frustrated when we take the car to a mechanic who not only fixes the problem we knew about but also takes the liberty of repairing other problems (and charging liberally for them). In short, we want (and expect) to be served according to our preferences and felt needs. Innocuous enough when it comes to the morsels on our plates, the reign of personal preferences involves more serious implications when it extends over the rest of life. And in the life of faith, the consequences are serious indeed. For preference-driven faith will, in the end, produce a Christless Christianity. Have It Your Way What do we hope for when we join the church for worship? Parsing motives presents no easy project, especially if there are children in tow or responsibilities for some aspect of the service or fellowship. Few of us have the personal or cognitive space to search out the depths of our hearts en route to the Sunday morning service. But the way home often presents opportunities to interrogate those hidden recesses. The questions we pose shed light on what is in our hearts: “How did you like the sermon this morning?” “Didn’t the worship team nail it today?” We tend to ask not about a confrontation with gospel truth but about measures of personal satisfaction. If our questions begin illuminating this tendency, the answers we give put our motives on clear display: “I thought the pastor did a great job! I really liked . . .” or “Ya know, I just wasn’t feeling it this morning; the sermon didn’t really speak to me.” “Yes, the worship was great!” or “I thought the team was a bit off. Did you hear them mess up on that one song?” So often, whether at the sandwich shop or on the way home from church, preference-driven language bubbles out of our mouths like boiling water from an unwatched pot. For many, our post-service concerns center far too frequently on how well certain aspects of the service met our felt needs. What did I gain from the sermon? Did I enjoy the music? Service to the ascendant self predominates. We reflect on the worship gathering in a manner unsettlingly similar to how we might reflect on a hamburger: It was decent, but I’ve had better elsewhere. I think they overdid the mayonnaise, and I would have preferred sesame rather than a brioche bun. Whether we want to admit it or not, our expectations of being served as we please spill into our perceived relationship to the church’s gathered worship. Those same expectations shape how we approach our Lord. We tend naturally, in our sin, to want merely an affirming savior. We like to hear that Jesus loves sinners so much that he died to win them, for hearing this affirms that our need for forgiveness has been met. We like to hear that his love for his sheep never falters, for hearing this quells the fear that perhaps our snide words or dubious choices or the train wreck of our inner thoughts might put our hope in jeopardy. We like to hear how our Lord railed against the hypocrisy and legalism of the Pharisees, for hearing this makes us smile inwardly, pleased that we are not so pretentious and uptight. Messages such as these leave us content, unruffled, ready to carry on with life as normal, affirmed in our preferred way of life by a (truncated) gospel that accomplishes little b

content: “Hey, honey, you’re not going to be able to sleep tonight if you don’t start shutting things down soon!” After 36 years of marriage, my husband knows me well. He’s absolutely right, but I still sometimes want to keep pushing until bedtime. The way of wisdom is to stop consciously, set the work aside, and engage in the repetitive, mundane wind-down of the day. The work will still be there tomorrow, and I can trust God for new mercies to finish when morning comes (Lamentations 3:22–23). Our habits of rest reveal what we trust. While our need for sleep, recreation, and downtime weighs on our very physical, very finite bodies, we often resist submitting to our limitations. Substituting entertainment for true rest, we become passive consumers of endlessly streaming content that devours our time. Paradoxically, we crave rest and engage in ceaseless striving after things we hope will satisfy the desires of our heart. This is an ongoing battle for me, and I know I’m not alone. Our society values activity and busyness. We spend our hours and days going and doing, always with one eye on the clock. We reward tireless resilience with job promotions and earnest admiration. In our fervor for achievement, we may forget that rest is necessary for quality work to continue — and that rest can teach our hearts to trust God. Rest Reveals the Heart Psalm 127:1–2 is a reminder for our caffeinated and sleep-deprived souls that progress depends not solely on the work of our own hands but on God’s gracious provision: Unless the L ORD builds the house, those who build it labor in vain. Unless the L ORD watches over the city, the watchman stays awake in vain. It is in vain that you rise up early and go late to rest, eating the bread of anxious toil; for he gives to his beloved sleep. Note that the psalmist illustrates a right and a wrong way to work. He makes three important points for the restless. 1. The Lord builds the house. God builds the ministry, the family, and the career. We work in cooperation with the Lord, and he watches over us and our work. The point is not that we shouldn’t work heartily at whatever we do (Colossians 3:23). Rather, our security is found in God, not in our efforts. Knowing our frame, remembering that we are dust, God commands us to observe regular patterns of rest, not only for our physical health but also as an acknowledgment of our dependence upon him (Psalm 103:14). 2. The Lord watches over the city. Whether we’re closing our eyes or closing our laptop and office door at the end of the day, when we leave the results of our work in God’s hands, we demonstrate trust in him. “He who keeps Israel will neither slumber nor sleep,” the psalmist writes (Psalm 121:4). God is your keeper, too. Entrusting our work to the Lord prevents it from becoming an idol. In our glad contemplation of work well done, we remember that he is both giver and gift. Our work is evidence of his power and goodness. 3. The Lord gives sleep to his beloved. Anyone who has spent a night sleepless from worry knows our bodies are not designed to run on anxious adrenaline. Insomnia has many causes and may not indicate a spiritual problem, but God often uses physical symptoms to reveal our spiritual condition. A steady diet of “the bread of anxious toil” (Psalm 127:2) starves us of what we need most: the ability to rest in God. When we rest, we accept our God-given limits. We hand the controls over to him. We lay aside our disordered loves, and we choose to believe the Father’s delight in Christ is also for us, his treasured children: “This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 3:17). Because it can feel entirely unnatural, we may need to approach rest as a learned behavior, a habit of holiness, a spiritual discipline that we “put on” in the same way Paul exhorted the Colossians to clothe themselves with compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness, and patience (Colossians 3:12). Such discipline is worth the effort; when we rest, we proclaim

title: What We Get Wrong About the Tears of Jesus
summary: Was Jesus’s grief at Lazarus’s tomb over his friend’s death or the response of the mourners? Pastor John explains how Jesus’s perfect emotions captured his indignation over unbelief. Listen Now
content: Audio Transcript “Jesus wept” (John 11:35). It’s the shortest verse in the Bible. We read it together in the Navigators Bible Reading Plan yesterday. But it’s so brief we can pass it too quickly. Maybe we pass over it because we think we know what it means. Jesus’s friend Lazarus died. Jesus wept because his friend was gone. But what if we got that wrong? Or, what if we mistakenly thought his emotions were simple when they were complex? What if Jesus wept not simply in the loss of death but from a frustration with the living? Today on Ask Pastor John: what we get wrong about the tears of Jesus. Henry, a listener, writes in with a timely question on John 11:35. “Pastor John, thank you for taking my question today. I’d like to ask you about John 11:35. Why do you think Jesus wept at the tomb of Lazarus? One way to read this account is that he’s simply sharing in Mary and Martha’s sorrows over his death. But I wonder if something deeper is going on here. Jesus already planned to raise Lazarus, and he even told his disciples he was going to do it in John 11:11–15. “So, my questions are these two: First, why does Jesus ask, ‘Where have you laid him?’ Was he simply asking to be taken to the tomb? When they answer, ‘Lord, come and see,’ it’s almost like they still don’t appreciate who he is as the Messiah. And that is my second question: This whole event leaves me wondering if this weeping is more like Jesus’s weeping over Jerusalem in Luke 19:41 — weeping because he is heartbroken over the city’s unbelief. Is it a stretch to connect these two moments? Is Jesus grieving the dead Lazarus? Or is he grieving the unbelief of the living?” Jesus’s Mingled Emotions I doubt that any of Jesus’s emotions were simple. I think they were always complex. We finite creatures have emotions that respond to one or two, maybe three, happy or painful aspects of a situation. So, we may feel sorrow and joy mingled because, say, a very old saint has just gone to be with the Lord, and we will miss him, and yet we’re so happy for him. But Jesus could see every angle, every imaginable aspect of a situation, some of which called for very different emotions. So, I doubt that he ever had a simple emotion. For example, in Mark 3:1–5, there’s this man with a withered hand in the synagogue, and the people are watching to see if Jesus would heal him so that they could accuse Jesus. Can you imagine? They don’t give a hoot about this man’s pain. All they want is to accuse Jesus if he heals him. And in verse 5, it says, “He looked around at them with anger, grieved at their hardness of heart.” And that’s what I mean by complex emotions: anger and grief perfectly mingled in the sinless heart of Jesus. Another example would be that he looked on unbelieving Jerusalem and wept: “Would that you, even you, had known on this day the things that make for peace! But now they are hidden from your eyes” (Luke 19:42). But in Luke 10:21, it says Jesus “rejoiced in the Holy Spirit and said, ‘I thank you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, that you have hidden these things from the wise and understanding and revealed them to little children; yes, Father, for such was your gracious will.’” He could weep and rejoice over the wise and bitter providence of God. So, we come to John 11 and the death of Lazarus. And I think Henry, who’s sending us this question, is right when he says Jesus’s tears in John 11 aren’t just about sharing our human grief — that maybe he is genuinely mourning their spiritual blindness. Yes, and I’m going to say not just mourning — he’s indignant. Divine Love and Wisdom The story begins in John 11:1–6 with Mary and Martha sending words to Jesus that their brother Lazarus is very sick. Jesus waits two more days before going and intentionally lets Lazarus die. He says in John 11:14–15, “Lazarus has died, and for your sake I am glad that I was not there, so that you may believe.” That’s an amazing statement: “I let him die for the sake of your faith.” “They needed to

content: Several times now, I have been out in creation with unbelievers, speaking to them of eternal matters, and, passing by a dying branch at the base of a tree, I have picked it up and said, “This is your life apart from Christ.” Speaking about their souls, Jesus’s illustration is irresistible. The conversation goes something like this: Jesus gives us this illustration. He looks you in the eye and says that he is the tree (to augment the illustration slightly), and you are the branch. Look up and see the branches above us, beautiful leaves waving, healthy in their vibrant greens, bearing evidence of life. And then there is this branch. Dry. Leafless. Withered. Why? Because it is detached from the source of its life. Cut off from the one it was made to have communion with. And so, it lies here, detached from its purpose and severed from the only thing that can make it flourish. Jesus claims to be man’s source. He claims to be the Tree to whom you belong. In relationship with him, you have life. Apart from him, he teaches, you spend life withering. I usually pause to let the claim have its proper space. I ask what they think of such an assertion. I give them an opportunity to respond. I have often expected indifference or offense, but I have consistently been met with quiet consideration or outright acknowledgment that such an illustration made sense to them. Or at least they would like to hear more. So I go on to wonder aloud with them. What is it like to be a branch fallen from the tree that is, as Jesus says, withering ? Don’t you know? Need we ask? The restlessness, the fatal dryness, the looming death. The reaching out to anything and everything for life — except for the tree standing beside and over us. Him we do not want. Him we can do without. We can make it our own way. The adverb is different, but the end is the same — restless withering, drunken withering, religious, secular, or thoughtless withering . Some overdose on pleasure. Others get high on their own morality. Still others distract themselves from death’s shadow creeping over them with fantasy football and rounds of golf. But for all that, withering. But Jesus himself asserts that he is the Tree. He is the one we were made for; in him alone can we find the life that haunts us in still and sober moments. Be grafted to him through repentance and faith, be attached to him by the Spirit of the living God, have his words live in you, direct you, amaze you, and dead things will come to life. And what will it be on that day, I am compelled to continue, for those dry and fruitless branches who refused life in him? They will be gathered and thrown into the fire and burned as useless things. But Jesus came that you might have otherwise. He told us his mission was to bring life — life abundantly . Imagine the branch grafted to the tree, suddenly infused with life and purpose and the vital sap of God’s own Spirit. We are as branches; the Father, Son, and Spirit are the source of everlasting life. With him, we flourish though all may seem to go poorly. Without him, only sapped wood remains. Would you like to know more about this Jesus? Now, I tell you this to highlight one of many places where the Bible addresses the interiority of man and its solution: God. I want you to see how dangerous the alternative answers found in modern therapeutic culture are to our souls and our churches. It is a scourge, especially to this inward age, not because a therapeutic culture takes distresses of the heart seriously, but because it too often sends branches reaching out for anything but the Tree. Ingrown Toenails The problem comes not from a focus on the inner man. Anyone who says the Bible has little to say about internal battles, demons, depressions, anxieties, doubts, and the despairs of human life should not air his ignorance. content: It was a great honor to be able to partner with Missionary to create Goers , a series of illustrated biographies for children. Each biography introduces young readers and listeners to the stories of men and women who were sent by churches to spread the good news about Jesus Christ to the ends of the earth. Each is illustrated by the ultra-talented Rommel Ruiz. The books can be purchased as a set of three or as individual volumes. The Plowboy’s Bible: The Story of William Tyndale’s English Translation . Hunted by spies, William Tyndale fled across Europe with a bounty on his head, his Bible translation labeled as contraband. Young John, on the other hand, has a long day of farm work ahead of him. Although their lives seem worlds apart, John’s father knows a story that binds John and William together—their love for God’s word. The scripture John relies on for encouragement cost William everything, but they gave John’s family everything! Rescued from Darkness: Amy Carmichael and the Girls of Dohnavur . Kumari is scared, helpless, and alone in a dark temple until Amma, a mysterious woman from a faraway land, carries her away to a beautiful garden. This is not a fairy tale. It’s the true story of missionary Amy Carmichael and the children she rescued and raised at Dohnavur Fellowship in India. Into the Unknown: David Livingstone’s Heart for Africa . Before David Livingstone was the most famous man in the world, he was a boy who dreamed of being free to explore God’s creation. But when David reached the mission field, he found that freedom taken from the people he tried to teach about the Creator. This is the story of a goer’s dangerous journey to the ends of the earth, of his courageous stand for justice, and of his patient endurance for the sake of Christ. The Goers series is written for children ages 4–10, and is ideal for parents to read to their children or for young readers to read on their own. Each book includes discussion questions and prayer points to get your family thinking and praying about the Great Commission. Each hardcover volume has 40 full-color pages and is sized 10″ x 10″. The Goers series is currently available exclusively through Westminster Books . Look for three more volumes to be added to the series around this time next year. content: Good morning. If you have read this site for any length of time, you will know that I am not the kind of person who does hot takes, since I just don’t trust myself to do them well. However, with the Wesley Huff situation developing, I did want to link to what I consider an especially helpful assessment of the matter. You can find that beneath today’s recommended reads. Sales & Deals Today’s Kindle deals include several volumes in the excellent New Studies in Dogmatics series. You’ll also find books by Jinger Duggar Vuolo, David Mathis, John Piper, and others. I continue to find and highlight hardcover and softcover book deals as part of Amazon’s Pre-Black Friday Book Deals . There are around 80 of them now, many of which are half off or more. Recommended Reading Hot Water and Holy Wonder: Giving Thanks for Ordinary Luxuries. “Every now and then, as I sit in my home library, a sense of awe settles over me—a spirit of wonder at the everyday comforts that surround me.” Trevin Wax celebrates the joy of the ordinary luxuries that God so graciously grants us. Are My Prayers Selfish? Responding to a question from a listener, John Piper explains the difference between prayers that are selfish and those that simply ask for things. “James is saying there is a kind of prayer that treats God like a cuckold. It refers to a husband whose wife is cheating on him. That’s a cuckold. Christians are making God into a cuckold. How? When it says they are praying just to spend it on their passions. The picture is of an unfaithful wife who asked her husband for $50 so she can go down the hall and pay another man to have sex with her. That’s the picture. She’s using prayer to cheat on her husband, God.” When the Heavens Declare: What a Solar Halo Says to a Secular City. Johannesburg was recently the site of a solar halo ( see here for images ). Tim Cantrell writes about what the skies were declaring in that moment. Gospel-Pilling the Looksmaxxers: Hope for Despairing Men. “What do dating apps, the 1999 film The Matrix, rhinoplasty, crystal meth, and smashing your face with a hammer all have in common? Welcome to the world of looksmaxxers. Let’s start at the beginning.” Mark Sanders introduces a concerning trend for young men and offers a much more satisfying hope. Here Are the Lessons I’ve Learned About Single Missionaries (From a Lifetime of Being One). I’m neither single nor a missionary, but still very much appreciate Andy Smith’s thoughts on the matter. “I always assumed that I would get married. I never thought I would enter full-time ministry. Yet, here I am, a contented single missionary since 1989.” Don’t Be Afraid to Provoke Your Brothers. Michael Kelley says why it’s important that we provoke one another. “I grew up in a house with two brothers. By the time we were all in school, ‘provoking’ was down to an art form. For each of my brothers, I knew the right buttons to push to get a rise out of them. I knew the words, the facial expressions, or even the subtle hint to drop that would flush their anger. What’s more, I knew how to do it to one of them to get at the other one. Like I said, an art form.” On Wesley Huff All those who have heard the recent news about Wesley Huff’s plagiarism have been shocked by it, myself no less than anyone else. I think Glen Scrivener is especially helpful, firm, and compassionate in this video . Even if you don’t watch it all, consider watching the final 10 minutes for the brief “sermon” he preaches there. Huff released a statement yesterday, which you can read on X or Facebook . Flashback The Blessing of a Higher Purpose in Our Pain. The chief end of affliction is to glorify God and enjoy him. The purpose of our lives is the purpose of our times of struggle, loss, grief, illness, and bereavement. The local church enables the world to look upon the canvas of God’s people and see an authentic painting of Christ’s love and holiness, not a forgery. —Jonathan Leeman Download Share See Also A La Carte (April 1) A L

content: I have been blogging at Challies.com on a daily basis for over 23 years now. That long commitment has allowed me to write thousands of articles and hundreds of book reviews while also sending millions of visitors to other sites through the daily A La Carte feature. Though I’ve also written a number of books, the blog has always remained the “main thing.” Much of the blog’s content is now also translated into Spanish , French , and a number of other languages. One of my great desires has always been to freely give away as much as possible. I intend for it to always remain entirely free for all who visit . While, for obvious reasons, this can’t happen when it comes to books, I’ve made it my goal to ensure that everything else has been freely and widely distributed. While this has been possible largely because of advertisers, there is also a key role for the generosity of individuals. This is where patrons come in—patrons like you. There are a couple of different options for you to consider. The first is recurring monthly gifts. A service called Patreon provides a convenient means of linking content producers (like me) with ongoing supporters (like you). You can learn more and sign up at Patreon.com/challies . I also share monthly ministry and family updates there. The second is one-time gifts. If that is of interest to you, they can be made electronically via PayPal . If you prefer to send a one-time gift via check, you can simply mail a check (drawn on a US or Canadian bank) to this address: Tim Challies 1011 Upper Middle Road East, Box #1214 Oakville, Ontario L6H 5Z9 Canada Funds donated will be used to support my family and to help create great content or to otherwise improve, support, and enhance Challies.com. In one way or another, they will all be used to allow me to continue to do what I have been doing for these past 23+ years. Please understand that I intend for Challies.com to always remain entirely free. In fact, patrons help ensure that it always remains that way. Thank you for considering becoming a patron of Challies.com. Your support means so much to me. And this is the end of my once-yearly mention of this subject! content: Thanks for reading A La Carte! I’ve got a good collection of articles, sales, deals, and other material for you this morning. I hope you enjoy it! Sales & Deals Today’s Kindle deals include a new edition of John Piper’s Desiring God , two reader-friendly studies in Romans from Tim Keller, The Gospel After Christendom , and my own From the Rising of the Sun (which, to remind you, includes the full documentary for free). Westminster Books is featuring my three Goers books for kids, each of which features a well-known Christian figure. They are nicely discounted. Logos users will want to check out Bible Study Week where you’ll find lots of deals, highlighted by the Tyndale OT & NT Commentaries at $4.99 each. Recommended Reading The Hardest Day You May Ever Face. This is a beautifully tragic piece of writing from Kimberly Wagner as she recounts an extremely hard day. “Daylight was just breaking over the ridge beyond the hills when I slipped into Mom’s bedroom and climbed into the bed beside her, the same bed that as a child I’d run to in the middle of the night to find safety and comfort. On this date, many years ago, we laid my dad’s body in the grave. But, Momma no longer remembers dates, or only guesses to know what season of the year we’re in. She won’t know the significance of today’s date, but she does have a foggy awareness that, to her today represents something terrible on her horizon.” For the Ones Like Me. Zachary Conover writes for those who are like him in that they were raised as good church kids. “What does it mean that we were dead in our trespasses and sins? How were we enemies of God? How were our hearts in rebellion against His Word? For students who have grown up attending church, reading the Bible, and learning about Jesus, these descriptions can be difficult to reconcile with their own experience. I understand that difficulty because I was one of those kids.” Praying to the God Who Rules History. Casey McCall reminds us that when we pray, we pray to the God who rules history. “If your doctrine of God leads you to pray less, you need to reevaluate your understanding of God. If your system of theology leads you to underemphasize the practical power of petitionary prayer in your life, you need to modify your system.” Dear Gen Alpha, Claude Wants to Turn You Into a Toad. Please, for the Love of All Things Human, Don’t Let It. Christina Bieber Lake warns members of Gen Alpha about what an all-out and unthoughtful commitment to Claude and other AI apps is likely to do to them. “In simple terms, we are moving from AI (Artificial Intelligence), which is about getting help processing information, to AGI (Artificial General Intelligence), which is about telling a machine what to do and letting it do it while you sit back and file your fingernails. Experts are saying that AGI will produce ten times the impact of the industrial revolution at ten times the speed.” Old Dogs and New Tricks. “I’m not opposed to the idea of people retiring after many decades of work. They have worked hard, so why not enjoy the fruit of their labor? But what I’ve found disquieting is the static nature that characterizes some retirements. I’ve seen some light, however, at the end of the tunnel and from where I stand, it doesn’t look like a train!” J.V. Fesko explains why he isn’t eager to retire, even if he does eventually withdraw from the front lines of work. Getting a Handle on Our Emotions. Writing for the Biblical Counseling Coalition, Esther St. John offers counsel on getting a handle on emotions, or, perhaps better said, stewarding them faithfully. A Great Error Respecting Duty I have often pointed out that Christians used to speak of duty far more often than we do today, since it was important to express and fulfill the duties God had given his people. You can read what William Plumer believed about duty in this brief quote from one of his works, A Word to the Weary . God’s people sometimes fall into a great error respecting their duty.

title: What Takes 20 Years to Build Takes 5 Minutes to Destroy
summary: I think we’ve all heard many variations of the adage, “It takes 20 years to build a reputation, but only five minutes to destroy it.” A good name that has been established through many years of honor, success, or skilled leadership can be ruined in a moment when an act of immorality comes to light. See Also A La Carte (July 2) The Sinner’s Opinion of Himself The True Character of Unbelief
content: I think we’ve all heard many variations of the adage, “It takes 20 years to build a reputation, but only five minutes to destroy it.” A good name that has been established through many years of honor, success, or skilled leadership can be ruined in a moment when an act of immorality comes to light. Until a couple of weeks ago, Jensen Huang seemed to be on top of the world. While Nvidia, the company he co-founded, had long been a Silicon Valley success story, the rise of AI had driven it to new heights of success and its CEO to new heights of prosperity. Nvidia became the most valuable company in the world, its market capitalization of nearly $6 trillion surpassing even Apple’s. Huang’s net worth soared to over $200 billion, making him one of the wealthiest men in the world and one of the richest men in history. His two children have advanced positions within the company and his wife of more than 40 years distributes vast sums of money through their charitable foundation. Huang carefully curated his reputation and, as is so often the case in Silicon Valley, his image, with his slick black leather jackets becoming his trademark. Today, of course, Huang is no longer CEO of Nvidia or anything else. He was forced to resign after it came to light that he had engaged in extramarital affairs with multiple women, one of whom is allegedly a Chinese spy and another of whom is reportedly a subordinate within Nvidia. His image was shattered in a moment, and his reputation is now in tatters. The company lost over half a trillion dollars of value in the aftermath—value that was subtracted from Huang’s wealth, of course, but also from that of everyday investors whose wealth is far more modest. Pictures of his wife and children were splashed all over the news, and stories about his exploits were printed in every major media outlet in the world. The harm to his reputation is beyond repair, yet must pale in comparison to the harm and shame he has brought to his family. I hope that as Huang ponders what has become of his life, he has the wisdom to ask this: was it worth it? I hope each one of us asks the same, for Huang is not the first person to be tempted to grave sin , nor the first to succumb to temptation. In different ways and to different degrees, that is a battle we all fight every day. I have no experience of committing adultery, but I understand that it is exhilarating, and that doing what is forbidden delivers a great rush. And I suppose it must be exhilarating, for why else would a person risk so much to pursue it? Why else would a person do something that so defies common sense? Why else would a person gamble everything for the sake of illicit, fleeting pleasures? News reports describe him, in his final days at the company, calling himself “a piece of [expletive].” And while I wouldn’t phrase it that way, he’s not wrong that this situation has exposed him as what he truly is, and it’s actually far worse than the way he describes it. I might choose the word “wretch” to describe him, and not just him, but all of us. We are all wretches, for we are all wretched, people who trade short-term pleasure for long-term pain and fleeting joys for enduring sorrows. Sin makes us act like madmen, for sin is madness. And it leaves us wretched—desperately unhappy and in the sorriest of states. There has never been a sin that was more wise than foolish. There has never been a sin that delivered more gratification than the satisfaction of obedience. There has never been a sin that was worth more than the honor of a good name and an upstanding reputation. Thankfully, there has never been a sin that is beyond Jesus’s capacity to forgive. Though time and again we, like Huang, succumb to temptation, time and again Jesus forgives those who humble themselves before him to confess their sin and ask his forgiveness. May we all have the wisdom to see ourselves in Huang and to see in him a vivid example of the reality that sin promises joy while delivering sorr

content: Good morning, my friends. The God of love and peace be with you today. Sales & Deals Today’s Kindle deals include a couple of daily Advent devotionals, Greg Koukl’s Street Smarts , David Gibson’s Living Life Backward , Dane Ortlund’s Deeper , and more. You’ll also find some academic titles from Zondervan Academic. If you prefer printed books, remember that there’s a big Pre-Black Friday sale happening now. I added lots of new books to the list yesterday. There are many great deals to be had! Recommended Reading Remembering John Allen Chau. P. R. Swain remembers and honors John Allen Chau. “There has been plenty of discussion around John’s level of wisdom and preparedness. Many feel these were lacking. I will admit that landing on an island whose inhabitants are known to be violent toward outsiders is unwise. The wiser thing would’ve been for him to invest his savings in a mutual fund for forty years. How short-sighted of him. In the words of one of the five in Ecuador who preceded him in martyrdom, ‘He is no fool who gives what he cannot keep to gain what he cannot lose.’ John was no fool.” How to Experience Gospel Transformation. This is a tremendous article from Nicholas McDonald on practicing repentance. “Here is my encouragement to you, as you learn to practice the prayer of reconciliation. Take 5-10 minutes each night, and try to choose one thing (not a million things) that needs repentance from your day. It’s very important that you go beyond just naming your sin to God, here. It’s important to name your sin (even out loud!), but that’s not going to transform you. What will transform you is learning to practice reconciliation with God, through the gospel.” The Quiet Voice. Catherine Mackenzie was one of those people who enjoyed the quiet that came to her life when Outlook crashed. “Although almost everything I had planned that day depended on email, and almost none of it got done, I actually talked to my colleagues. We caught up properly, in a way our inboxes don’t usually leave room for. I sat beside the designer instead of messaging her on Teams, and we all shared jokes and discussed our favourite period dramas.” She goes on to draw some observations from the marriage of John and Polly Newton. What We Get Wrong About the Tears of Jesus. John Piper addresses (and corrects, I suppose) a misplaced emphasis when it comes to a famous story from the life of Jesus—weeping outside the tomb of his friend Lazarus. I Thought Adultery Had Been Approved. David Hall writes about the downfall of Jensen Huang and the hypocrisy it unveils. “But, wait, is the NVDA board composed of pastors, puritans, and other assorted backwoods Baptists or something? I thought adultery had become widely acceptable. How can a company part with such a genius merely because of consensual sex out of marriage? Supposedly, this was a victimless crime that should not inhibit the rise of super duper intelligence, especially earning trillions.” The Singularity Will Never Happen. Some people are concerned that with the rise of AI we are heading to the point of singularity, but Justin Poythress explains why that will never happen. “We know the future will look dramatically different, but we’re only beginning to conceive the ways in which AI will reshape it. There is one thing Christians can know with certainty. It’s a knowledge which should equip Christians to lead the way in quelling the anxiety about this new world we’re hurtling toward. The Singularity … will never happen.” Videos Worth Watching What Is the Christian View of Suicide? Kevin DeYoung answers a common question during a Q&A. 50 Difficult Theology Questions Answered in 50 Minutes . Adriel Sanchez answers a whole lot of questions in a short format. Among them are questions like these: Is America in the end times? Why are there so many different denominations? Are Mormons and Catholics Christians? Why does evil exist in the world? Why Does Jesus Speak in Parables? Daniel Stevens explains why Jesus rel

title: This Week in Christian Books (November 17, 2026)
summary: This is a big week, thanks largely to Christian Focus, which releases its whole November list in one go. It also brings a new edition of J. I. Packer’s Truth and Power, Matthew Westerholm’s Biblical Worship, Randy Alcorn’s major book on what the Bible says about animals, and the newest volume in the Reformed Expository Commentary. See Also This Week in Christian Books (November 10, 2026) New and Notable Christian Books for October 2026 (Plus a Preview of November) This Week in Christian Books (O
content: Tuesday is the day most publishers release their new books, so each week I let you know what has just come our way from the publishers I follow most closely. This is a big week, thanks largely to Christian Focus, which releases its whole November list in one go. It also brings a new edition of J. I. Packer’s Truth and Power , Matthew Westerholm’s Biblical Worship , Randy Alcorn’s major book on what the Bible says about animals, and the newest volume in the Reformed Expository Commentary. There are also several new academic works and a number of books for children. In each case, I’ve included the publisher’s description. Books for Everyone Crossway Biblical Worship A Christ-Centered Practical Theology Matthew Westerholm Endorsed by: Thomas R. Schreiner, Ryanne J. Molinari, Joseph R. Crider, Brian J. Tabb, and Zac Hicks Publisher’s description Humans are made to worship, but as sinners, the most we can offer God is imperfect praise. In the Old Testament, people used various symbols and rituals to show devotion, but these flawed offerings would find their ultimate fulfillment in Jesus, the perfect worshiper. So, what should biblical worship look like for redeemed people today? Matthew Westerholm gives churches a unified vision for worship by studying its different expressions throughout salvation history. First, he presents a biblical theology of worship from Genesis to Christ. Next, Westerholm defines proper worship as acknowledging God’s creating power, generous faithfulness, and purposeful commission. Finally, he offers readers practical guidance about where, when, and how to worship today. Written to encourage the entire congregation, this book celebrates how Christ’s atoning work transforms worship from ritualistic obligation to joyful expression. Buy it at Amazon or Westminster Books . Christian Focus Shattered Dreams and God’s Plan The Joseph Narrative in Genesis 37–50 Dale Ralph Davis Endorsed by: Sam Emadi and Harrison Perkins Publisher’s description Dale Ralph Davis gives us a rich, pastoral exploration of Joseph’s story—where shattered dreams, hidden providence, and unshakable grace collide. With clarity, wit, and deep theological insight, Davis brings Genesis 37–50 to life, showing how God works through chaos, silence, and suffering to accomplish his purposes. Perfect for personal study, preaching, or group discussion, this book invites readers to see their own struggles through the lens of God’s faithful plan. Whether you’re navigating your own “Genesis 37” season or seeking a deeper understanding of Scripture, Shattered Dreams and God’s Plan will strengthen your faith and renew your confidence in the God who never abandons His plans—or His people. Buy it at Amazon . IVP Truth and Power The Place of Scripture in the Christian Life J. I. Packer Endorsed by: Kevin J. Vanhoozer, Ray Ortlund, Trevin Wax, and Tom Nelson Publisher’s description In a world full of theological upheaval and trendy philosophies, Truth and Power ’s bold challenge for the church to remain committed to Scripture is as relevant today as when it was first written. Through centuries of use, abuse, and disuse, the Bible remains the foundational document of the Christian faith. From J. I. Packer, beloved theologian and author of Knowing God, Truth and Power explores how the Bible should shape every aspect of Christian discipleship. In this time-tested and masterful overview of the doctrine of Scripture, Packer offers both lifelong believers and new Christians thoughtful, personal guide to understanding Scripture’s rightful place in the Christian life. In Truth and Power , Packer explores the true place, use, and benefit of the Bible in the Christian life; examines Scripture’s authority, methods of interpretation, and its role in preaching, the church, and the life of the individual believer; invites you to move from a shallow cultural Christianity to a vibrant faith that testifies to the truth and power of God’s Word; and helps Christians rightly valu
author: Tim Challies

title: A La Carte (November 17)
summary: Classroom apologetics / Can we legitimately judge a person’s faith? / Lord, why am I still here? / The world is always burning / Frank Peretti and the 40th anniversary of This Present Darkness / The best way to serve your local church / Kindle deals, new books, and more See Also A La Carte (February 10) A La Carte (May 26) A La Carte (October 1)
content: I was glad to return home safely after an extremely enjoyable weekend in San Diego with the men of Compass Bible Church. It was a fitting end to my speaking engagements for the year. I’m now settled back into my home office to get cracking on some major book projects. Sales & Deals Today’s Kindle deals include a variety of books, and among them you’ll find a couple of relatively new titles from P&R: Pray with Your Eyes Open and You Are Not Alone . You’ll also find Mark Vroegop’s ultra-popular Dark Clouds, Deep Mercy and several other options. Recommended Reading Classroom Apologetics. I think you’ll be encouraged to read of Joshua Budimlic’s extraordinary experience in a Canadian public school classroom. “In the Lord’s timing, the morning of September 11th, 2025, was the day I taught my first lesson to a class of Grade 11 Law students—Charlie Kirk had been murdered the day before. As you can imagine, Charlie’s death overshadowed any plans I’d previously made to open my lecture with a discussion of 9/11 and its lasting implications, or the then-recent murder of Iryna Zarutska on a North Carolina light-rail train just a few weeks prior. It was only the second week of the new school year, and already the darkness was beginning to gather.” Can We Legitimately Judge a Person’s Faith? Stephen Kneale answers an important question: Can we legitimately judge another person’s faith? He explains why this is not merely legitimate, but necessary. “We all know liars exists, wolves do run around and many, though no doubt sincere, can be self-deceived. Some Christians can be quick to take every word at face value and easily fooled whilst others, albeit often out of sincere motive, lead people to believe in unbiblical theology and gospels full of half-truths that can leave genuine people further away from Jesus than they realise.” Lord, Why Am I Still Here? Peter Witkowski: “Few questions can appear as esoteric and yet prove as profoundly practical as the question: ‘Lord, Why am I still here?’ It is a question that seminary students with little life experience can talk over into the early hours of the morning as they sip energy drinks. It is a question that the newly minted widower feels throughout the recesses of his soul as he selects a coffin for his beloved bride. And it is a question that Jesus answers…” The World Is Always Burning. Andrea Sanborn is correct: it does feel like the world is burning right now. Yet in some ways, it is always true that the world is burning. “Does it seem like the world is burning to you? From droughts to floods, wars and riots…sometimes it feels like we are falling apart. Like we are falling apart from each other. From common sense or sanity, even. From God. It’s disconcerting, certainly. Flat-out frightening at times. At best, we live with a low-level anxiety humming in our spirits, wondering how close the flames will creep to our homes. The truth is, the world has always been burning. Burning up. Burning down. Only now, technology allows us to witness the flames in every corner.” Frank Peretti, the 40th Anniversary of This Present Darkness, and Memories From Years of Friendship. I perhaps don’t feel quite as positive about This Present Darkness as Randy Alcorn does, but I still enjoyed reading about his friendship with Frank Peretti. It’s hard to believe that the book is 40 years old! The Best Way to Serve Your Local Church. “‘I really want to find a way to plug in and serve the church.’ I overheard this comment about a decade ago as a church member spoke to one of our pastors. I loved the sincerity and desire of this brother, but I wondered what our pastor was going to say. I leaned in and listened extra close because I was genuinely curious.” The answer was a good one. New Books New Christian books tend to release on Tuesdays. Here are just a few of the books that have become available today. For a more thorough list—and there are tons of new releases this week—visit This Week in Christian Books . All God
author: Tim Challies

title: No Condemnation
summary: Featuring thousands of study notes drawn from the bestselling NIV Application Commentary series, the NIV Application Bible helps you understand Scripture and connect it to your world in a whole new way. It guides you in discovering how the ancient truths found in Scripture relate to your experiences today using insight from trusted evangelical scholars, paired with timely biblical application principles. Read an excerpt on the blog. See Also Free Stuff Fridays (HarperCollins) Using the NIV Zonde
content: This week, the blog is sponsored by Zondervan and this article is adapted from the NIV Application Bible . Text in bold is taken from the application notes on Romans 8:1 in the NIV Application Bible. Beneath the outer veneer of our lives, many of us live with a layer of guilt and shame. We feel like we’re not good enough. We want to be good Christians, but we just don’t feel like we are. Perhaps we sit in church surrounded by people who seem to have their lives more together than ours and who seem to lead better Christian lives than we do. This feeling leaves us anxious and ashamed, unsure of where we really stand before God. Let Romans 8:1 fill you with hope: “There is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus”! Because we are justified by faith in Christ, we escape the sentence of spiritual death that our sins have earned. We have been transferred into the new realm of life. Because we have believed in Jesus’ finished work for us on the cross, we no longer have to fear that our sins will ever condemn us. Once we are walking with Jesus, we walk by faith and depend on grace rather than our own works. Our hope is not in what we have done or in what we can do, but in what God has done in Christ Jesus through his death and resurrection. If we are in Christ, there is no condemnation. If God does not condemn us, we must not go on condemning ourselves. Instead, we walk in the freedom and joy of God’s grace, led by God’s Holy Spirit.
