title: Who or What? A Continuum for Using AI Wisely
summary: From AI as god to AI as assistant. Here is a continuum of nine roles that can help Christians tell legitimate uses of AI from illegitimate ones, and wise from unwise. See Also A Christian’s Guide to AI Technology is Fast, Sanctification Is Slow, and Claude Can’t Do It For You A La Carte (October 16)
content: It is sometimes hard to believe that it has been only four years since AI became widely available. Few technologies have made so massive and rapid a leap into our daily lives, to the extent that AI now exists in the background of all of our lives and, for many of us, in the foreground as well. Few technologies have evolved as quickly, so that the latest ChatGPT model bears about as much resemblance to its debut as the latest MacBook does to a Commodore 64. If all this has happened in just four years, imagine what the next four—or the next fourteen—might hold. As AI’s capabilities have increased, so too have the ways we can use it in our homes, churches, and workplaces. It seems like every month or two we read of a feature that can make a difference to our lives by adding a new ability or taking on work that used to be done by a person. The latest trend is the rise of agents—AI tools like Meta’s Muse or xAI’s Grok Bot that can carry out tasks, routines, and duties on an ongoing basis. With all of the tools available to us and all of their capabilities, it can be difficult to know which uses are legitimate and which are not. We all know that just because AI can do a task doesn’t mean that it should . So how can we determine the legitimate roles AI can play in our lives? I think sketching out a continuum of some of AI’s potential roles can help us. At the beginning are roles that most of us would agree are illegitimate, and at the end roles that most of us would agree are legitimate. Between them are roles that may be illegitimate in some cases and perfectly fine in others. These demand that we approach them thoughtfully to determine whether integrating them into our lives would be an act of wisdom or folly. As you will see, illegitimate roles tend to be those that require a who whereas legitimate roles tend to be those that require a mere what . The Continuum AI as God . There are some people, most of them deeply engaged in the tech industry, who ascribe to AI god-like qualities and who relate to it accordingly. They may believe it is an evil god that is likely to destroy humanity or a benevolent god that is likely to redeem humanity, but in either case, they treat AI as something far more than software. These people go too far and commit idolatry as they attribute to tech what rightly belongs to God. AI as Friend . There are some people who relate to AI as a friend, and even a few troubled people who relate to it as a lover. While AI is capable of mimicking the kind of relationship one might enjoy with a fellow human being, it can only ever mimic it. To relate to AI as a friend is to anthropomorphize a mere technology and worse, to deprive oneself of actual friendship. Though AI can imitate friendship, it cannot be a friend in any legitimate sense of the word, for friendship depends upon personhood. Not only that, but friendship depends upon mutuality and both the blessings and risks that come with relationship. You cannot be friends with AI any more than you can be friends with a tree, a PlayStation, or any other non-being. AI as Counselor . Many people today relate to AI as a counselor—a confidant who will listen patiently and counsel them with a trusted voice. Yet because AI is a what , not a who , it cannot offer answers based on a true understanding of their circumstances, true wisdom that comes from learning and experience, or true compassion that comes from sharing their humanity. It cannot empathize with them, pray for them, or plead with the Holy Spirit for wisdom in helping them. AI is capable of advising in many ways, but not of counseling, for counseling is inherently personal. AI as Pastor . Increasingly, people bring to AI the matters of spiritual health, growth, and well-being that in the past would have been addressed to a pastor. Every Christian needs to be under the loving oversight of a pastor who will care for their soul, and such crucial matters must be entrusted not to AI, but to a pastor who is called and
author: Tim Challies

title: Arrested at the hospital where he worked, he turned the prison into a pulpit
summary: 🇪🇷Eritrea· 2010s
content: Dr Berhane was a new believer in Jesus, working in a hospital in Eritrea, when the secret police came for him. His crime was his faith. They put him in prison for eleven months, in one of the harshest systems on earth, a place designed to make Christians disappear and go quiet. He did the opposite. "Every day I was clapping my hands," he said, "and prisoners would come forward and I shared the gospel." A man who had only recently met Jesus decided his cell was simply the next place to introduce Him. Three Bibles and a valley of death The authorities took his Bible. He smuggled another in. They took that one too, and he smuggled a third. He leaned hard on the Psalms, and when fellow prisoners were taken out and executed, the old line about walking through the valley of the shadow of death stopped being poetry and became the thing that held him upright. Eleven months of that did not break him. It made him a preacher. The guards meant to silence a new Christian and instead handed him a congregation with nowhere to go. Wherever they put you, Jesus goes with you, and He is not intimidated by the walls. Dr Berhane found that out in an Eritrean prison. You can trust it wherever you are.

title: A construction engineer in Madagascar became convinced the Bible was true
summary: 🇲🇬Madagascar· 2013
content: Melias was building things for a living in Madagascar, a construction engineer with a steady trade and, by his own account, no particular expectation that God would interrupt him. In 2013, at twenty-one, God did. It was not dramatic thunder. It was quieter and harder to argue with. "The Holy Spirit convinced my heart that the Bible is true," Melias said. "I found new joy and excitement learning about Jesus through the Scriptures." The book he might have dismissed became the most alive thing in his life. From building houses to building the church He could have kept his new faith as a private comfort and gone on with engineering. Instead he gave it everything. In 2015 he trained for six months as a missionary, and since then he has planted churches and discipled new believers among the Tanala people in Ikongo and the Sakalava in Nosy Be, some of the least reached corners of the island. Now he is training three more Malagasy missionaries to do the same. Madagascar is not a footnote in what God is doing. He is raising up local people like Melias, engineers and tradesmen and ordinary workers, and sending them to their own unreached neighbours. When the Holy Spirit convinces your heart that this is all true, it does not stay a hobby. It becomes the thing you build your life around. He is ready to convince yours.

title: A New Testament sat in his welding workshop until a teenager finally read it
summary: 🇳🇪Agadez· 2000s
content: Someone left a New Testament in Pierre's welding workshop in Niger, and for a while it just sat there. He was a teenager, and eventually he picked it up. What he read did not match what he had been told about Christians. It was full of tenderness, of nearness to the poorest, exactly the kind of world his young heart had been quietly hoping was real. Years later he moved to Agadez, out toward the desert, and there he found the thing the book had described. A church family drawn from Benin, Togo, Burkina Faso, France, and Niger, living out what he had only read about. No regret, not for a single day Pierre became a lay missionary, and he does not hedge when he talks about it. "I have never regretted converting to the Christian faith," he says, "not even for a single day." That is a bold thing to say in Niger, where jihadist groups make following Jesus dangerous and his own children have stayed Muslim, something he carries with love and without pressure. Still, no regret. Not one day. He read about a God who is tender toward the poor, and he found that God to be exactly as advertised. Whatever you have heard about Jesus secondhand, He holds up when you finally meet Him yourself. Pierre would tell you to open the book and see.

title: He was taught Christians do not pray. Then he watched his uncle pray before a meal
content: Charles Yabaga Diarra grew up in a strict Muslim family in Lere, Mali, where Christians were mocked and misunderstood. His father, a headmaster and politician, ran the house like a school. As a boy, Charles fled about a hundred and fifty miles to stay with an uncle, and there he ran straight into something he had been told did not exist. His uncle, a Christian pastor, bowed his head and prayed before the meal. Charles was stunned. "Because we are Christians, we pray before meals," the uncle explained. Charles had been taught that Christians do not pray at all. That simple prayer, in his own language, lodged in him and would not leave. Just show me the way His father pulled him back and forced him into Quranic school, but the seed was planted. Years later, back with his uncle, tired and searching, Charles finally prayed his own prayer. "Lord, I'm really tired of seeking the truth. Just show me the way." A verse he had heard at a Vacation Bible School came back to him, and in November 1981 he gave his life to Jesus. The cost has been real. Charles is a preacher now, displaced by Mali's conflict and facing daily pressure. But he did not go alone. Of his fourteen siblings, most now follow Jesus, and around a hundred Christians gather at his extended family events. One uncle praying over dinner turned a whole family toward Jesus. Your quiet, ordinary faithfulness may be planting more than you know.

title: A widow heard the good news from a travelling salesman and could not unhear it
summary: Laos· 2022
content: Pei was a fifty-two-year-old widow in Laos, raised the way her whole village was raised, worshipping ancestors and local spirits in a place where the government pushes atheism and neighbours warn that following the God of foreigners will offend the gods of home. Then a salesman came through and, somewhere between selling his goods, told her about Jesus. Salvation as a gift, not a payment. Pei believed it. She let go of the ancestor worship she had carried her whole life and quietly followed Jesus instead. The cost at her own front door She was discipled in secret for four months, growing strong enough to speak. The first people she told were her daughter and her son-in-law, who happens to be a policeman. They did not celebrate. He threatened her, saying that if she did not stop believing in Jesus, they would report her, jail her, or throw her out. In June they made good on it, tossing her clothes into the yard and telling her to go live with the people who gave her this Jesus. She went. She did not go back. A widow with nothing chose Jesus over a roof, because she had found something no one could evict from her heart. Following Jesus is not always safe, but it is always worth it. What Pei found is worth more than what it cost her, and it is offered to you too.

title: After his daughter was killed, he prayed for a Bible no one could take from him
summary: Uzbekistan and Tajikistan· 2020s
content: Rashid Kadirov was a Muslim in Central Asia when the worst thing happened. His six-year-old daughter Azizza was killed by a drunk neighbour driving a tractor. In his grief he went looking for something the ache could rest on, and he went to the Koran. There he read a line, in Surah 5:70, that pointed back to the Gospels as holy scripture. So he prayed a strange, specific prayer. He asked God for an Injil, a New Testament. His friends brought him one. It was a stolen Gideon Bible, taken from a vandalised car. It did not last. When the friends took it back, Rashid prayed again, this time for a Bible no one could take away from him. The book that stayed Then a couple arrived from Tajikistan, sent by a former classmate of his who had himself come to Christ. They carried a Bible and a copy of the JESUS Film. Rashid and his wife Aleka watched it, and as the good news was explained, each of them, without telling the other, quietly prayed to receive Jesus. Aleka barely understood it all. "She had very little understanding of the Gospel," she said later, "and yet peace flooded her heart." They were baptised in Tajikistan, and Rashid started telling others what he had found. A grieving father asked for a book, and God gave him a Person. The peace Rashid could not manufacture arrived the moment Jesus did. He is close to the brokenhearted, and He is near to you.

title: 35 priests could not help her. In a church she saw Jesus crush what was choking her
summary: 🇱🇰North Central Province· 2021
content: Chandra lived in a rural village in Sri Lanka's North Central Province, and she was slowly falling apart. Pain, weakness, a heart that raced for no reason doctors could name. She and her family were Hindu, so they did what they knew to do. They went to priest after priest. Thirty-five of them. Nothing changed. In July 2021 they walked into a church instead. As people prayed for her, Chandra saw something. Demons were trying to strangle her, and then Jesus Christ stepped in and stamped on them. She felt the pain and the sickness drain out of her body as they were defeated. In the vision Jesus spoke Scripture over her, from Psalm 34. "They looked to Him and were radiant," He said, and told her she would be radiant too if she trusted Him. The prayer a father prayed Her husband Dinesh, a day labourer, watched his wife come back to life and made God a promise. "God, if you will heal my wife, I will dedicate my daughter for your service." The whole family, who had barely heard the name of Jesus, gave their lives to Him. Their daughter Tenusha told her class what had happened, that her mother was free and that Jesus forgives sinners and makes them new. They did not keep it to themselves. A house church started in their home with four people. By now it is forty-six. Jesus is still stronger than whatever is choking the life out of you. He steps in, He stamps it down, and He calls you radiant.

title: He prayed for his mother's infected leg. Then his Muslim neighbours started coming
summary: 🇸🇩El Hasahisa· 2022
content: Pastor Abdalla Haron Sulieman gathered his small church in El Hasahisa, Sudan, to pray for his mother. Aisha Adam was sixty, and a leg infection had worn her down. They prayed, and she recovered. What looked like a private family mercy did not stay private for long. Word of the healing moved through the town, which is mostly Muslim. And people started showing up at the church. Not to argue. To ask if the God who healed Aisha might heal them too. When a healing becomes a door That is exactly the kind of thing that makes some people afraid. Local extremists pressed the police to arrest Sulieman, and they did, charging him under an old law with claiming to be a witch doctor, as if the love of Jesus were a kind of sorcery. Believers across Sudan shared his name and called for his release. "This is a serious violation against Christians in Sudan," said one, an evangelist named Francis Ismail. But notice what the fear could not undo. A mother was well. A Muslim town had seen the name of Jesus do something real, and neighbours who had never entered a church walked in looking for Him. God still heals, and He still uses one ordinary answered prayer to open a door no one can shut. He can open one where you are too.

title: Karma said he had to earn heaven. At 17 he heard he could be forgiven
summary: Rakiraki· 1990s
content: Simon Gounder was born into a strict Hindu family in Fiji. His great-grandfather had been shipped from India as a contract labourer after the British took the islands in 1874, and the family settled in a small village in the north of Viti Levu. Simon grew up inside a system with clear rules. "As a Hindu, we believed in karma," he said. "If you do good karma, you get to heaven. If you do bad karma, you will be punished." It was a ledger he could never quite balance. He knew his own wrongs too well. The night the ledger closed At seventeen, a friend invited him to a Christian youth meeting in another town. There he heard something that did not fit anything he had been taught. That Jesus Christ could simply forgive sins. Not offset them, not average them out over lifetimes. Forgive them. Simon felt the weight of his own failures and, for the first time, an offer to be free of them. "I gave my life to Jesus that night," he said. He hid it from his parents at first. When they found out, they were not happy. But the son who came home changed did not stop there. In time he led his whole family to Christ, and he went on to plant a ministry that carries the same forgiveness to others. Karma keeps a running tab you can never clear. Jesus tears the tab up. Whatever you are carrying tonight, He is still in the business of forgiving it all at once.

title: A soldier who should have died in battle walked into a demon's shrine
summary: 🇲🇲Myanmar· 2010s
content: Pastor Dano was a soldier before he was a pastor. He came out of the battlefield alive when he had no reason to, and he never shook the sense of why. "I believe God preserved my life from death on the battlefield for a purpose," he said. The purpose showed up in a Buddhist village that wanted nothing to do with him. The vice chief's son was tormented, demon-possessed, and no one could help. Dano fasted and prayed for three days. Then, near midnight, he went to the shrine where the boy was and did the only thing he knew to do. "I called upon the name of the Lord," he said, "and the demon left the young man." The night the shrines fell silent Villagers said every evil spirit left the village at once. Dano went from shrine to shrine, praying against the darkness that had ruled the place for generations. The vice chief's family, who had braced for his anger, found grace instead. They gave their lives to Jesus, and four more families followed. The people who once opposed him now follow his lead. There is a church in that village today where there used to be shrines. The name of Jesus is still stronger than every dark thing that has ever frightened you. One believer, praying at midnight, was enough to set a whole village free.

title: They locked the pastor in a psychiatric ward. He led a hundred men to Jesus
content: Pastor Bakhytzhan Kashkumbaev was an elderly man when Kazakhstan arrested him in May 2013. The charges were strange, that he had harmed a church member's health and stirred up religious hatred. They sentenced him toward ten years and put him in a psychiatric ward, where inmates were routinely drugged. On the way in, he thought it might be the end of his mind. "This is probably the last time I will talk to you in my right mind," he said. Then a question reached him, the kind God uses. "Where is your faith?" Under the cover of the risen Lord Something lifted. "I felt like I was under the cover of the risen Lord," he said. The old man who expected to lose himself instead found Jesus nearer than the walls. He started talking to the men around him. To a prisoner wrecked by drug addiction he said simply, "Only Jesus can help you." Over nine months inside, nearly one hundred inmates gave their lives to Christ. "In prison," he said, "the Holy Spirit opened one dimension of prayer to me." The place meant to break him became the most fruitful pulpit of his life. They released him in early 2014. He walked out having planted the good news in the last place anyone would look for it. God is not locked out by any door that locks you in. He was already inside, waiting.

title: Her church offering came to the exact amount of her power bill, to the penny
summary: 🇺🇸United States· 2020s
content: Lina Johnson did not have enough to cover her power bill. She had told no one the amount. Not a friend, not her church, no one. It was her private worry, the kind you carry quietly and hope somehow resolves. That same week an offering came around at church for a family in need, and Lina gave what she could. Twenty-six cents. It was almost nothing, and she gave it anyway. Down to the penny The next day a friend told her the rest of the story. The offering the church had taken was for her. And when they counted it, it came to the exact amount of her power bill. To the penny. "The offering they took in church yesterday was for me," Lina said, "and it was the exact amount as my power bill. It was to the penny and I never told anyone how much my bill was." Here is the detail that undoes you. Had she given more than her twenty-six cents, the total would have overshot the bill, and the provision would have lost its edge. Even her small gift was part of God's arithmetic. God is not rounding up or guessing. He knew the number she never spoke aloud, and He met it precisely, through people who had no idea. The Father who counts the hairs on your head knows your bill too, down to the last penny.

title: He carried a bomb into a church. The sermon was about loving your enemies
summary: 🇮🇩Jakarta· 2000s
content: Ahmad Quraisy was a commanding officer in a militant Islamist group in Indonesia. The economic collapse of the late 1990s had radicalised him, and he blamed Christians for what had gone wrong. So he built a plan. He carried a time bomb into a Protestant church in Jakarta, intending to kill everyone inside. Then he heard the pastor preach. The man was telling his congregation to love their enemies and to pray for the people who persecuted them. Quraisy froze. "I never saw that Christian love before in my life," he said. He could not do it. He carried the bomb back out. His own leaders locked him up for a month for failing. The love he could not detonate That was only the beginning. In the year that followed, Quraisy began having visions he was sure came from Jesus. He was healed of typhus. His wife, unknown to him, had been quietly praying. By 2001 he gave his life to Christ. The man who wanted to blow up a church now builds them. Quraisy leads an underground network of around seven thousand former Muslims meeting in house churches across Indonesia, most of them still keeping a low profile to stay safe. The love that stopped his hand in that church is the same love reaching for you. It is stronger than the worst thing you ever planned to do.

title: He survived the killing fields. Then he baptised the man who ran a death camp
summary: 🇰🇭Cambodia· 1980s-1990s
content: Christopher LaPel grew up near the royal palace in Cambodia and wore a small ivory cross as a boy, though his father disapproved. Then the Khmer Rouge came. In 1975 he was driven into the labour camps, working sixteen-hour days in the fields. He lost both parents, a brother, and a sister to execution and starvation. He nearly died himself. When he was too sick to work for three days, soldiers came to execute him, and one of them looked at him and said he really looks sick, and walked away. He survived into a refugee camp in Thailand, empty and grieving. There a missionary told him that Jesus Christ had died on the cross for his sins. "This is the answer I've been waiting for," LaPel said, and he gave Jesus his life. The general who said, my sin is so deep LaPel became a pastor and went back to teach his own people. In 1995 a quiet man calling himself Hang Pin came to one of his leadership trainings. He gave his life to Christ, was baptised the next day, and began leading a house church. Only later did the world learn who he really was. Kang Kek Iew, known as Comrade Duch, had run S-21, the prison where around twelve thousand people were tortured and killed. He came to LaPel and said, "My sin is so deep." Duch surrendered to the authorities and was sentenced to life in prison, where he wore out the Bibles LaPel kept sending him. The man who survived the killing fields carried the grace of Jesus back to one of the men who built them. No sin is too deep for the blood of Jesus. Not the worst thing done to you. Not the worst thing you have done.

title: A witch doctor got a solar radio. It was tuned to the truth
summary: 🇨🇬Democratic Republic of Congo· 2010s
content: Mbutu was a witch doctor in a remote village in the Democratic Republic of Congo. For years he cast spells, claimed power over the natural world, and sold cures to sick villagers who had nowhere else to turn. People feared him. He made his living off that fear. Then he was given a small solar-powered radio. It was fixed to one station, a local Christian broadcast, and handed out to villagers who had no other way to hear anything. Tuned to the truth So Mbutu listened. Day after day the good news came through that little speaker. He learned of the One who really controls the universe, and more than that, he learned about the love of Jesus and His offer of forgiveness. The man who had traded in fear laid his witchcraft down and gave his life to Christ. He did not keep it to himself. Mbutu now walks from village to village, finding other witch doctors and telling them what he found. Some of them have become believers. Some have become pastors, planting churches where there were none. A cheap radio and the name of Jesus were enough to turn the most feared man in the village into its brightest light. No one is beyond the reach of that name. Not the person others are afraid of. Not you.

content: En cette solennité des saints Pierre et Paul, patrons de la ville de Rome, la basilique Saint-Pierre est au centre de l’attention de tous la population de la ville ce 29 juin 1633. On y présente en effet pour la première fois au public le gigantesque Baldaquin de bronze commandé neuf ans plus tôt par le pape Urbain VIII à Gian Lorenzo Bernini, dit Le Bernin. Dans la matinée, les barrières et les échafaudages qui masquent la structure, sous la coupole, sont retirés. La structure est massive, unique en son genre. La foule accourt alors. Et la curiosité du peuple n’est pas motivée uniquement par la réputation de l’architecte, qui commence à se faire un nom, à 34 ans, et s’impose comme le favori du pape. Ce baldaquin démesuré, on en parle depuis des mois. Le commanditaire de l’œuvre, le pape Urbain VIII (Maffeo Barberini), célèbre lui-même la messe de la Saint-Pierre-et-Paul sous ce nouveau dais. title: From Post-Punk to German Techno—A Musical Journey
summary: By Mark Ellis — Known for his scholarship, journalism, and voice, Brian C. Nixon has another creative life—one that spans more than three decades of songwriting, recording, and musical exploration. Nixon is perhaps best known for his academic work at Veritas International University, his books, and his journalism for God Reports, ASSIST News Service, and other media […]  The post  From Post-Punk to German Techno—A Musical Journey  first appeared on  God Reports .
content: By Mark Ellis — Known for his scholarship, journalism, and voice, Brian C. Nixon has another creative life—one that spans more than three decades of songwriting, recording, and musical exploration. Brian Nixon Nixon is perhaps best known for his academic work at Veritas International University , his books, and his journalism for God Reports , ASSIST News Service , and other media outlets. His voice has also reached listeners across the country through his former involvement with the radio program To Every Man an Answer (later known as Pastors’ Perspective ) and, more recently, Paratus , a program devoted to developing a biblical worldview. What may surprise those familiar with Nixon’s academic and journalistic work is that he is also an accomplished musician and songwriter whose musical journey spans more than 30 years. In his forthcoming book, A Beautiful Defense: How Aesthetics Points to God , co-written with Dr. Patrick Zukeran and scheduled for release in 2027 , Nixon explores the relationship between beauty, faith, and the creative process. In anticipation of the book’s release, I spoke with Nixon about his musical beginnings, his creative influences, and his unexpected venture into German electronic music. Tell me about your early musical journey. I grew up in a musical family. Music was part of my everyday life. During high school, I formed a band with some friends that eventually signed with an independent record label in the San Francisco Bay Area. We released only one record, but several of the other members went on to successful careers in the music industry. One became involved in founding Stones Throw Records, an influential independent label known for its underground hip-hop and experimental music. It was an exciting time. We were young, creative, and discovering what music could be. What did you do after the band broke up? I continued my college education, eventually transferring to California State University, Stanislaus. There, I met another group of musicians, and we formed a band called Canterbury. We ended up winning a Bay Area battle-of-the-bands competition, which was exciting. But rather than continuing in that direction, we decided to pursue something with a more intentional ministry focus. That led to the formation of Widow’s Mite . Widow’s Mite eventually signed with Rick Wakeman, the legendary keyboardist of Yes. Interestingly, that connection also introduced me to journalist Dan Wooding, who wrote Wakeman’s first biography. That relationship eventually opened the door for me to write for ASSIST News Service . So, in a rather unexpected way, my musical career helped launch my journalism career. Widow’s Mite After college, did you continue writing music? Absolutely. I still write music today. My compositions range from jazz and pop to what I call tone poems —short instrumental works that emphasize mood, atmosphere, and musical expression. Some are experimental, while others are much more accessible. I’ve always enjoyed exploring different musical forms rather than staying within a single genre. Interestingly, some of my recent compositions have been selected for rotation by a German online radio station. And here’s the surprising part: they’re German electronic and techno-influenced songs. I’ve been experimenting with AI-assisted production, including using a synthesized female vocalist to interpret my compositions. Did you say German techno? (Laughs.) I know. It sounds funny, doesn’t it? But there’s a story behind it. Recently, I took a deep dive into the music of Kraftwerk, the pioneering German electronic band. I was familiar with their work during high school in the early 1980s because they had influenced so many of the post-punk bands I was listening to at the time. I decided to revisit their entire catalog, and I was blown away all over again. They were years ahead of their time. Their approach to rhythm, synthesizers, repetition, and technology helped shape entire genres of contemporary music.

summary: By Charles Gardner — My wife Linda had no idea of the Jewish background of her employers during the 1970s and 80s. So we travelled down to London for an exhibition of the Salmon and […]  The post  Discovering Jewish roots, responding to antisemitism  first appeared on  God Reports .
content: By Charles Gardner — Charles and Linda on their wedding day My wife Linda had no idea of the Jewish background of her employers during the 1970s and 80s. She just knew that she loved working for them and only left to follow God’s call to work with children. So we travelled down to London for an exhibition of the Salmon and Gluckstein dynasty, and the story of how these resilient Jewish families fled violent persecution in Eastern Europe to build what became the largest catering company in the world known as J Lyons & Co. Linda worked there as a home economist from 1977-1984 but it was only much later that she learnt of the Jewish nature of the firm that once literally fed Britain with its teashops and corner houses on every high street, and its products in every home, Linda playing her part through her cooking and marketing skills. A few years later, after graduating from Bible College in Bournemouth, she worked at a prayer and reconciliation centre in Northern Ireland where she was introduced to the importance of the Christian faith’s Jewish roots, as a result of which she took a study tour of Israel to learn more. And on a second trip to the Holy Land ten years later, she got more than she bargained for. At Cana in Galilee, where Jesus turned water into wine at a wedding, Linda was given a vision of her own wedding. And we met on a blind date six months later! Though having Jewish ancestry myself, I grew up knowing nothing about it. But I learnt more later, especially after becoming a Christian in my early twenties, as Linda had done. It helped that I had a Jewish believer as my early mentor, and I became increasingly aware of the significance of our Jewish heritage, about which I now write prolifically. Meanwhile Linda, who has been teaching Christianity in Doncaster area schools for over 30 years, also now teaches about Judaism as it forms the context into which Christ came to us, fulfilling all the laws and promises of the Old Testament. So in both our cases, we were kept in the dark about very important aspects of our lives – until the Lord shone his light on the truth. Which brings me to the Christian Church as a whole, especially in the UK. We have known very little, if anything, of our faith’s Jewish roots or of God’s ongoing purposes for Israel. This needs to change – and fast! For we are surely hurtling towards the Messiah’s Second Coming like a high-speed train, in danger of coming off the rails with the rest of humanity if we fail to get to grips with how we Christians fit into the unfolding picture of global opposition to tiny Israel. What is our role as we watch antisemitism spread across the globe like wildfire? Do we just sit and watch, or write it off as having nothing to do with us, and remain silent? Or do we stand up to be counted as those who refuse to salute the new Nazism that portrays itself as anti-Zionism – a Confessing Church walking the way of the cross for God’s chosen people? My questions come as renewed calls are made for an independent inquiry into antisemitism at the BBC following news that Oscar-winning producer Lucie Kon has won £400,000 in compensation from the broadcaster. Lucie’s career is said to have unravelled after she raised concerns about antisemitism within the BBC, though the latter have not admitted to any fault. This is highly significant as millions of UK Christians are (where Israel is concerned) probably more influenced by what they hear from our national broadcaster than what they read in the Bible. title: New senator from Michigan says he’ll take oath on Quran
summary: By Howard Cooper — Abdul El-Sayed, the Michigan Democrat who became the first Muslim elected to the U.S. Senate, says he plans to take his oath of office on a Quran when the new Congress convenes in January. El-Sayed, 42, defeated Republican Mike Rogers on November 3, becoming the first Muslim American elected to the […]  The post  New senator from Michigan says he’ll take oath on Quran  first appeared on  God Reports .
content: By Howard Cooper — Abdul Al-Sayed (wikipedia commons) Abdul El-Sayed, the Michigan Democrat who became the first Muslim elected to the U.S. Senate, says he plans to take his oath of office on a Quran when the new Congress convenes in January. El-Sayed, 42, defeated Republican Mike Rogers on November 3, becoming the first Muslim American elected to the Senate and the first epidemiologist to serve in the chamber, according to WION News. In an interview with NPR’s Leila Fadel, he said, “I will likely swear on a Quran. Which Quran, we’re not sure.” He pointed to a copy once owned by Thomas Jefferson, which Keith Ellison used when he was sworn in to Congress, and to an old Quran at the University of Michigan that he described as the first in the state. The US Constitution does not require a Bible or any religious text. In practice, senators usually take the formal oath together on the Senate floor, and a Bible comes into play in individual ceremonial swearings-in. El-Sayed hasn’t said whether he’ll use the Quran in the formal proceedings, the ceremony, or both, and that his choice would not alter the wording of the oath. He has also stressed that his oath will be to the U.S. Constitution,  according to IBTimes. He will be sworn in by Vice President JD Vance, a fact El-Sayed has noted with humor. The Blaze reported he called it a “delicious irony” that Vance is constitutionally required to do so. Not everyone is comfortable with the news. The Daily Signal reported that former White House press secretary Sean Spicer said this week that given El-Sayed’s connections and statements, he should undergo a formal background check before receiving classified information. Presumably, Spicer was referring to Al-Sayed’s family connections to the Muslim Brotherhood. For many Christians, the moment raises questions about the role of faith in public life, the long American tradition of religious liberty, and the Judeo-Christian roots of the United States. El-Sayed and his colleagues are scheduled to be sworn in at noon on January 3, 2027. The post New senator from Michigan says he’ll take oath on Quran first appeared on God Reports .

summary: By Charles Gardner — A brave Yemeni journalist has stunned the United Nations with an account of how his view of Israel has dramatically changed following a visit there. Luai Ahmed was invited to […]  The post  Yemeni journalist visits Israel, dramatically changes views  first appeared on  God Reports .
content: By Charles Gardner — Luai Ahmed speaking at UN (screenshot YouTube) A brave Yemeni journalist has stunned the United Nations with an account of how his view of Israel has dramatically changed following a visit there. And he was led to the conclusion that everything he has been taught to believe about the Jews is a lie. Luai Ahmed was invited to address the assembly by UN Watch, a non-governmental organisation monitoring the international body’s performance, as the UN Human Rights Council gathered to debate racism. He said: “I grew up in Yemen, where the word that we used for black people is ‘abeed’, which quite literally means ‘slaves’. Racism towards black people in my country is horrifying, but it’s not even the most toxic hatred that I was taught. “The first time I ever heard the word ‘Jew’ was in my local mosque when I was nine years old. At the end of Friday prayers, the Imam said: ‘May Allah kill the Jews and the Zionists’. And I responded alongside thousands of Muslims praying beside me: ‘Ameen’.” Luai then continued: “I was taught that Zionism meant killing Arabs, stealing our land, and destroying Islam. Then October 7th came. Hamas terrorists ‘freed Palestine’ by slaughtering 1,200 Israelis and kidnapping more than 200 people, including a one-year-old child. “Almost everyone in my Arab-Muslim circle celebrated. I didn’t. Instead, as a journalist, I decided to visit the so-called Zionist entity, and I was completely shocked to the core by the lack of apartheid and racism that I experienced. “One day, I got an eye infection. At the hospital, the nurses in reception were Jewish. The doctor treating me was Arab. Is there racism in Israel? Of course. There’s racism everywhere. “But Arabs in Israel aren’t called ‘slaves’. They are doctors, engineers, and party leaders. My experience helped me realise that Zionism really just means the Jewish people’s right to a tiny country. Everything I was taught was a lie.” Quite apart from tipping over the tables of woke left-wing ideology spreading its poisonous antisemitic tentacles across the globe, Luai’s testimony also knocks holes into the escalating pressure on the UK to make reparations for the slave trade, which saw plenty of collaborators in the host countries of those who suffered. And of course, the truth that dare not speak its name – that it was Christians like William Wilberforce who put an end to it! Luai is a great inspiration to fellow journalists like me who long for more of our colleagues to stand up and be counted. Thanks also to David Soakell of Christian Friends of Israel’s Watching Over Zion newsletter, November 5, 2026. title: Manta ray led marine scientist to lost fin
summary: By Mark Ellis — Growing up in Laguna Beach, California, Amber Sparks developed a deep love for the ocean, which led her to study marine science at UC Berkeley and earn a master’s degree at Scripps Institute in San Diego. As co-founder of Blue Latitudes Foundation, she works with industry to find opportunities for conservation, […]  The post  Manta ray led marine scientist to lost fin  first appeared on  God Reports .
content: By Mark Ellis — Amber Sparks (Blue Latitudes Foundation Facebook page) Growing up in Laguna Beach, California, Amber Sparks developed a deep love for the ocean, which led her to study marine science at UC Berkeley and earn a master’s degree at Scripps Institute in San Diego. As co-founder of Blue Latitudes Foundation, she works with industry to find opportunities for conservation, especially with the Rigs-to-Reefs program, when oil drilling platforms are decommissioned. “We work with the oil companies to repurpose certain parts of the platform, retrofit it so that it can remain in place and continue to function as an artificial reef,” she told God Reports. Amber’s work has taken her around the world, with many dive experiences and encounters in the ocean with marine life. But there is one story she will never forget. It happened in the Gulf of Mexico shortly after Amber graduated from Scripps Institute and was invited on a research industry cruise with oil company representatives, scientists, and regulators on a liveaboard vessel. At the Flower Garden National Banks, a marine protected area 200 miles offshore, Amber was excited about her first dive, but slightly nervous. “You don’t know what you’re going to see or what this experience is going to be like,” she recalls. Dropping in (Blue Latitudes Foundation Facebook) Each diver had to jump off the vessel to get in the water. “We’re all geared up with our snorkel, our buoyancy control device, our wetsuit, and fins are the last thing you put on. So, I put on my fins and I jumped off the side of the boat.” “The second that I hit the water, one of my fins fell off, and I looked down and watched as it slowly descended to the bottom.” Amber glanced over at her dive buddy, and said, “I’m gonna go down. I’m going down.” Normally she would wait for her dive partner and they would go down together, but in this case, she thought, “I can’t (wait). I gotta go get my fin.” So Amber slowly began to descend to the bottom, about 60 feet below the ocean surface. “I felt completely lost. I was in a completely new area. I never dove before, and now I only had one fin.” She realized there were major currents that could have moved her fin in any direction. “I realized I can’t really swim with just one fin. So now not only am I at depth, but I’m handicapped with just one fin, and I started to feel pretty nervous.” It would probably take her 10 minutes to get back the surface, with safety stops. At the moment before panic set in, she looked upward and saw an amazing sight. It was a giant manta ray, with wings extending at least 10 feet. “Its wingspan was double mine. Its arms were out, and it was coming up over the side of a reef. “I’ve never seen a manta ray like this before. It totally took my breath away, it was so magnificent.” Another manta ray (Blue Latitudes Foundation Facebook page) She noted that manta rays are known in the ocean community to be “majestic, God-connected creatures with an understanding maybe beyond what humans can fully comprehend. They see the world and feel it in another way,” she notes. Mantas have the largest known brain of any fish. Their brains are large in absolute terms and relative to body size, which is also true of elephants, dolphins, and people. Their brains have enlarged areas associated with intelligence, vision, and motor coordination, and some of their brain cells are more like those in birds and mammals than in other fish.(1) As the manta ray drew close to Amber, she had an unusual communication experience. “I felt this sense where it said, ‘I want you to follow me. I’m going to help you find your fin.’ Amber Sparks Amber’s diving partner had just descended next to her, and they both began to swim after the manta. “I was barely making it, following this manta ray across the reef. At this point, I was so excited to see a manta ray. I kind of forgot about being handicapped, and I was just trying to go as fast as I can to keep up with it. Then Amber got the sur

content: The word epiphany is defined by the Oxford Learner’s Dictionary as “a sudden and surprising moment of understanding.” Often, such epiphany moments arrive unexpectedly, interrupting the ordinary rhythms of life with extraordinary insight. Sometimes they come through a conversation, a passage of Scripture, or an encounter with nature. Other times, they emerge through art. Twilight Epiphany. Photo: Eliott Davis Sitting beneath artist James Turrell’s Twilight Epiphany on the campus of Rice University in Houston, Texas, on a Sunday morning as the sun rose, the word epiphany took on new meaning. As the morning light slowly illuminated the sky, subtle shifts in color transformed the space above me. The experience was both architectural and atmospheric, a convergence of art, nature, and contemplation. Turrell, born in 1943, is an American artist internationally recognized for his exploration of light, space, and human perception. Raised in the Quaker tradition, Turrell’s artistic vision reflects an appreciation for silence, stillness, and inward reflection. Commissioned by Rice University through the generosity of alumna Suzanne Deal Booth, Twilight Epiphany opened in 2012 as part of the university’s public art program. The pyramidal Skyspace, designed to accommodate approximately 120 visitors, features an aperture in its roof through which viewers observe the changing sky. At sunrise and sunset, carefully programmed LED lights interact with the natural atmosphere, creating an extraordinary experience of shifting color and perception. More than a work of architecture, the installation invites visitors to slow down, look upward, and reconsider the relationship between light and the world around them. James Turrell (Chat GPT) For me, the experience was something of a spiritual exercise. Light, after all, is among the Bible’s most enduring metaphors for divine revelation, truth, and beauty. As the colors shifted above me, I was reminded that beauty does not always announce itself loudly. Sometimes it simply asks us to be still and pay attention. Rothko Chapel. Photo: https://www.mark-rothko.org/rothko-chapel.jsp#google_vignette. From Rice University, I headed to another meditative landmark: the Rothko Chapel . Here, I sat among the monumental, dark-hued paintings of Mark Rothko, contemplating both the tragedy of the artist’s life and the triumph of the chapel that bears his name. Commissioned by Houston philanthropists John and Dominique de Menil in 1964 and dedicated in 1971, the Rothko Chapel is an interfaith sanctuary devoted to contemplation, spiritual reflection, and human rights. Its octagonal interior contains fourteen large-scale paintings by Rothko, whose subtle variations of black, maroon, and purple create an atmosphere of profound stillness. Rothko, born Marcus Rothkowitz in 1903, was a leading figure in American Abstract Expressionism, celebrated for his ability to evoke deep emotional responses through color and form. Yet his personal life was marked by physical illness, depression, and emotional turmoil. In February 1970, before the chapel’s dedication, Rothko died by suicide at the age of sixty-six. He never witnessed the completed sanctuary that would become one of his most enduring artistic legacies. Twilight Epiphany. Photo: Brian C. Nixon There is something deeply moving about this juxtaposition. An artist whose life ended in despair left behind a place where countless visitors have sought peace, meaning, and solace. The darkness of Rothko’s paintings does not necessarily communicate hopelessness. Rather, their quiet intensity invites viewers to confront the depths of human experience—sorrow, longing, mystery, and perhaps even transcendence. Where Turrell’s Twilight Epiphany draws the eyes upward toward the heavens, Rothko’s chapel seems to draw the gaze inward, toward the mysteries of the human soul. One is animated by the changing light of the sky, the other by the stillness of darkened canvases. Yet both offer some

title: Lanier’s Sixth Annual John Warwick Montgomery Lecture Series: A Grand Success
summary: While sitting in the John Warwick Montgomery Study Center at the Lanier Library and Study Center in Houston, Texas, awaiting a meeting, I turned to librarian Sharon Cofran and Executive Director Dr. David Fleming and remarked, “John Warwick Montgomery would be very pleased with what Lanier has accomplished on his behalf.” From Montgomery’s framed correspondence […]  The post  Lanier’s Sixth Annual John Warwick Montgomery Lecture Series: A Grand Success  first appeared on  God Reports .
content: John Warwick Montgomery While sitting in the John Warwick Montgomery Study Center at the Lanier Library and Study Center in Houston, Texas, awaiting a meeting, I turned to librarian Sharon Cofran and Executive Director Dr. David Fleming and remarked, “John Warwick Montgomery would be very pleased with what Lanier has accomplished on his behalf.” From Montgomery’s framed correspondence with C. S. Lewis and his barrister gowns to the thousands of books that comprise his remarkable personal collection, Lanier has provided the Christian world with a marvelous tribute to one of the great Christian intellectuals of the twentieth and twenty-first centuries. Born in 1931, John Warwick Montgomery (d. 2024) was a distinguished Christian apologist, theologian, attorney, and scholar whose extraordinary career spanned several disciplines. Holding numerous academic degrees, including doctorates in theology, philosophy, and law, Montgomery became internationally recognized for his defense of Christianity through historical evidence, legal reasoning, and philosophical argumentation. His influential books, including History and Christianity , Faith Founded on Fact , and The Shape of the Past , helped establish a rigorous approach to Christian apologetics. Whether lecturing in universities, debating skeptics, or practicing law, Montgomery maintained that Christianity was not merely a matter of subjective belief but a faith grounded in historical reality and rational inquiry. Yet to stop at the library would be to understate Lanier’s remarkable work. The sixth annual John Warwick Montgomery Lecture Series was a tour de force of distinguished thinkers, passionate Christians, and intellectually engaging presentations. More than a commemoration of Montgomery’s life, the gathering represented a continuation of his intellectual legacy: the conviction that Christianity can withstand serious scrutiny and offer compelling answers to life’s most profound questions. Mark Lanier, Nancy Pearcey, Paul Gould, Adam Francisco, and Michael Horton From the opening panel discussion hosted by attorney and philanthropist Mark Lanier to Dr. Paul Gould’s thoughtful presentation on worldviews, followed by attorney Craig Parton’s lecture on jurisprudential apologetics, one theme emerged with unmistakable clarity: Christianity is a reasonable faith. The presentations reflected Montgomery’s own interdisciplinary approach to apologetics: the Christian faith and intellectual inquiry need not be adversaries. Indeed, the Christian tradition has long insisted that faith and reason are complementary avenues in the pursuit of truth. The following day continued this rich intellectual exploration. Professor Nancy Pearcey addressed questions surrounding truth, dismantling various modern ideologies, while Dr. Adam Francisco offered an informative overview of Islamic history and belief, helping participants better understand one of world’s biggest religions. The keynote address by Dr. Michael Horton examined the challenge of reaching those who identify as “spiritual but not religious,” a growing segment of contemporary society. Horton’s presentation underscored the importance of communicating historic Christian truth in a culture increasingly suspicious of religious institutions yet often deeply interested in spiritual meaning. Dr. Michael Horton On Sunday morning, Lanier founder, Mark Lanier, hosted many participants during his Biblical literacy class, where he continued the dialogue with Michael Horton. Taken together, the lectures, discussions, and interviews demonstrated the breadth of Christian scholarship and the continuing relevance of thoughtful apologetics in an age of skepticism, religious pluralism, and cultural uncertainty. As I reflected on the weekend, I was reminded of the Festschrift Christianity for the Tough-Minded , a collection of scholarly essays honoring Montgomery’s life and ministry. Like that volume, the Lanier lecture series brought together diverse intellec

content: What do Jesus and Isaiah have in common? Quite a bit, according to renowned British New Testament scholar N. T. Wright. Gathering at the marvelous Lanier Theological Library in Houston, Texas—the brainchild of noted attorney, author, and biblical scholar Mark Lanier—Wright offered a packed house in the Great Room a fascinating glimpse into the relationship between the Old Testament prophet Isaiah and the life, ministry, death, and resurrection of Jesus Christ. Dr. Joseph Holden of Veritas International University listening to Dr. NT Wright at Lanier Library. For Wright, Isaiah is far more than an ancient prophetic voice whose words occasionally appear in the New Testament. Rather, the prophet provides a theological framework for understanding Jesus and the unfolding purposes of God. In his book Into the Heart of Isaiah , Wright invites readers to rediscover the extraordinary depth of Isaiah’s prophetic vision, demonstrating how its themes of judgment, restoration, redemption, and new creation find their ultimate expression in Christ. Central to Wright’s interpretation is the conviction that Isaiah’s message cannot be separated from the larger story of Israel. The prophet speaks of exile and homecoming, divine judgment and covenant faithfulness, suffering and salvation. These themes, Wright argues, become essential to understanding how Jesus understood his own mission and how the earliest Christians interpreted his life. Particularly significant is Isaiah’s portrayal of the suffering servant, whose affliction becomes the means through which God’s redemptive purposes are accomplished. Wright connects this prophetic imagery to Jesus’ sacrificial death, while emphasizing that the cross cannot be isolated from the broader biblical promise of God’s restoration of creation. Equally important is Isaiah’s vision of a renewed world, a creation in which justice, righteousness, and peace flourish under God’s reign. For Wright, the resurrection of Jesus announces the beginning of that promised new creation. The Christian hope, therefore, is not simply an escape from the present world, but the ultimate renewal of God’s good creation. Personal Stories: Mounting Up with Wings Like Eagles Amid the theological insights and biblical exposition, Wright shared several personal stories, offering the audience a glimpse into how the words of Isaiah have shaped not only his scholarship but also his spiritual imagination. One story centered on the beloved passage from Isaiah 40:31, in which the prophet declares that those who wait upon the Lord shall renew their strength and mount up with wings like eagles. Wright recalled preaching on Isaiah many years earlier and drew an amusing comparison to the long-running British radio program Desert Island Discs , in which notable guests select the recordings they would take with them if stranded on a deserted island. “I’ve sometimes said I have a set of desert island texts,” Wright explained, suggesting that certain biblical passages remain especially meaningful throughout one’s life. Near the top of his list, he said, is the closing portion of Isaiah 40, with its magnificent image of soaring eagles. The passage, he suggested, is more than a favorite theological text. It is part of his personal testimony, a biblical promise that has accompanied him through the years. A second story brought the imagery of Isaiah into an unexpected encounter with the natural world. While completing the final proofreading of Into the Heart of Isaiah , Wright and his wife, Maggie, were staying at their home in Scotland. Wright was alone in a room, carefully reviewing the text, when something outside caught his attention. “Out of the corner of my eye, I saw something,” he recalled. “At first, I thought it was somebody’s dog that had come into our front garden.” Noted Biblical archeologist, Dr. Steven Collins, listening to Mark Lanier interview Dr. NT Wright at Lanier Library. title: WWII Japanese POW found ‘freedom’ in camp
summary: By Charles Gardner — When a Japanese sailor’s destroyer was sunk by the Americans in a World War II South Pacific battle, most of his companions drowned. (Only 18 of […]  The post  WWII Japanese POW found ‘freedom’ in camp  first appeared on  God Reports .
content: By Charles Gardner — When a Japanese sailor’s destroyer was sunk by the Americans in a World War II South Pacific battle, most of his companions drowned. Amazingly, even though he was sucked underneath the waves with others as the ship went down, torpedo officer Michiharu Shinya somehow survived this 1942 disaster. (Only 18 of the 200-strong crew did). But he would rather have died at that point as his people had been indoctrinated to believe that it was shameful to be captured. Nevertheless, he was badly wounded but nursed back to health by medics. In time, he was picked up and eventually taken to a Prisoner-of-War camp at Featherston, near Wellington, in New Zealand, where he was to spend the next three years, as Don Stephens records in his inspirational book War and Grace (Evangelical Press, an imprint of 10Publishing). Shinya and his fellow inmates were treated with much kindness (in sharp contrast to the torture often experienced by Allied prisoners at the hands of the Japanese). Being showered with gifts at Christmas, a feast he knew nothing about, seemed especially strange. However, he was determined not to be ‘taken in’ by the Christian teaching offered after some of the prisoners requested spiritual help and a Japanese Bible was made available. That is until he chanced upon an article entitled ‘Sorrow in Victory’ in which the author quoted a ‘Hebrew prophet’ as saying: “Those who hope in the Lord will renew their strength. They shall soar on wings like eagles; they will run and not grow weary; they will walk and not be faint.” It made a deep impression on him, and he was determined to find out where it came from. Assuming it was from the Old Testament, he began reading the Bible, starting at Genesis chapter 1. Eventually, to his joy, he discovered that the profound words were from the Book of the prophet Isaiah (chapter 40, verse 31). After flagging somewhat in his search, he found himself hospitalised with malaria when a friend brought him a booklet called The Reason Why explaining the way to salvation. It so happened that the camp’s chaplain, Pastor Hessell Troughton, had been a missionary to Japan and spoke the language. Shinya joined others in his Bible studies and came to know and love Jesus as his Saviour. So much did this “complete freedom” now rule his life that prison had morphed into what he described as “a unique paradise on earth”. He never looked back after that and became convinced that his post-war calling would be in service of his Lord. When he finally returned home, his family were shocked to see him alive for he had been reported as killed in action. He had also given a false name to his captors because of the supposed shame of falling into enemy hands. Shinya subsequently became a pastor and prolific writer and translator following years of theological study both in Tokyo and the US. The Old Testament, he came to believe, demonstrated that sin is “the ultimate problem of mankind” and clearly pointed to Christ as the answer. On seeking to understand why so few Japanese became Christians, he felt it was partly due to their pride borne of believing they were a superior race. As for those three Christmases he spent in New Zealand, author Don Stephens writes: “Of all the gifts he received, the one he valued most was ‘the boundless and deep grace and peace of God in the Lord Jesus Christ’.” The post WWII Japanese POW found ‘freedom’ in camp first appeared on God Reports .

title: In the shadow of western stars: Grover Lewis, Larry McMurtry, and the triumph of words
summary: With The Grover Lewis Reader: Splendor in the Short Grass and Western Star, the newest biography of Larry McMurtry, in hand, I load my truck and head toward Archer City, Texas, accompanied by my wife, Melanie, and our friend Eliott. Archer City is, of course, McMurtry country, a small Texas town made famous through the literary imagination of […]  The post  In the shadow of western stars: Grover Lewis, Larry McMurtry, and the triumph of words  first appeared on  God Reports .
content: With The Grover Lewis Reader: Splendor in the Short Grass and Western Star , the newest biography of Larry McMurtry, in hand, I load my truck and head toward Archer City, Texas, accompanied by my wife, Melanie, and our friend Eliott. Archer City is, of course, McMurtry country, a small Texas town made famous through the literary imagination of one of America’s most celebrated novelists. Having written about McMurtry’s faith—or lack thereof—in a previous article , following an earlier visit to Archer City, I’m returning with a somewhat different interest. This time, my attention turns to Grover Lewis, the gifted journalist, critic, and poet whose life intersected with McMurtry’s during their college years. Lewis’ story, however, begins not with literary achievement but with almost unimaginable tragedy. As a child, he experienced the devastating loss of both parents when his father murdered his mother and was subsequently shot with the same gun, either by his dying wife or another person present. Lewis was only eight years old. It is difficult to imagine a more horrific beginning. Yet rather than allowing that tragedy to become the entirety of his story, Lewis eventually found a voice through literature. Perhaps the cards life dealt him gave him plenty to write about. Or perhaps writing became his way of making sense of a world that had revealed its cruelty far too early. In his autobiographical poem “Hillbilly Song,” Lewis writes: “You asked me once, Ann/Over coffee gone cold with talk/In your mother’s rain-drowsy/House, who they were, how it/Was with them in their breathless/Time in the wilds of years.” For Lewis, those early years were indeed wild. But they were also the soil from which his literary imagination would eventually grow. A Life in Words Born in Texas in 1934, Grover Lewis emerged as a distinctive voice in American journalism, particularly through his cultural criticism and reporting on the rapidly changing landscape of the 1960s and 1970s. He became known for his sharp observations, literary flair, and ability to capture the personalities and contradictions of American culture, even if he occasionally stretched the truth in the telling. His work appeared in prominent publications, including Rolling Stone , where his reporting helped establish his reputation as an insightful, sometimes cutting observer of popular culture. Lewis was more than a journalist, however. He was a poet and literary craftsman, someone who understood that words could do more than convey information. They could illuminate the human condition, expose its contradictions, and perhaps even provide a measure of healing. Grover Lewis (ChatPGT) Continuing “Hillbilly Song,” Lewis ponders: “At last, breathless and dry-mouthed/With private desire in the blue,/Swollen dark, we all lie down together—/My mother, my father, their perishing/Dreams, and I this unborn prisoner son…” There is something haunting about these lines. The dead remain present. The past refuses to disappear. And the poet, even as an adult, seems to wrestle with the circumstances that shaped his entrance into the world. Yet the very act of writing suggests something else: a refusal to remain silent. Two Texans, Two Literary Paths Lewis and Larry McMurtry crossed paths as students at North Texas State College, now the University of North Texas, during the 1950s. Both were young Texans drawn to literature and the possibilities of the written word. Their friendship developed within a shared intellectual environment, one that encouraged reading, conversation, and the pursuit of literary ambitions. Although their careers eventually followed different paths—McMurtry toward novels, screenplays, and literary fame, Lewis toward journalism, poetry, and cultural criticism—they shared an interest in the complexities of American life. content: Pastor Peter Colon portraying Major Rossvally in the movie of his story By Charles Gardner — A Jewish army surgeon was amazed by the courage of a young soldier badly wounded in the Battle of Gettysburg during the American Civil War (1861-65). Dr Max Rossvally was forced to amputate both a leg and arm in a bid to save the boy’s life. But it changed his own life. For the 17-year-old Drummer Boy – too young for frontline duty – refused chloroform or brandy to dull the pain. Charlie Coulson chose instead to trust in Jesus, his Lord and Saviour. The doctor – an army major and Orthodox Jew – was understandably stunned by the boy’s bravery, as well as his boldness in declaring his faith in Christ and imploring the officer (whom he knew to be Jewish) to put his own trust in Jesus, since he was also the Jewish Messiah. Max, however, was shaken rigid, and in a great dilemma, as he had always been taught to hate Jesus. For his people had largely rejected him as an ‘impostor’ and false Messiah. Charlie died just days later, apparently more concerned for the doctor’s eternal destiny than for his own painful exit from this life. Ten years later, Max found himself in a barber’s chair in New York once more being urged to trust in Jesus. Having explained the gospel, the barber promised to pray for him and said that, whenever he came in contact with a Jew, he felt it his duty to introduce him to the one who came for “the lost sheep of Israel” (Matthew 10:6). The surgeon subsequently boarded a train for a business meeting in Washington, where a newspaper advertisement drew him to a ‘revival’ service where the preacher echoed the messages he had heard from the barber and the boy soldier, leaving him in tears. He agonised at home in prayer for some time afterwards, struggling most of all with the thought that, if he accepted Christ, he would be going against all the advice and teaching he had known, not to mention the Jewish community as a whole. But he finally became convinced that Jesus was indeed the fulfilment of Old Testament prophecies (in particular, Genesis 49:10, Micah 5:2 and Isaiah 7:14). So he prayed: “O Lord God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. You know I am sincere in this thing. If Jesus Christ is the Son of God, reveal him to me this night, and I will accept him as my Messiah.” A long battle ensued, but his doubts were eventually replaced by joy and happiness as he praised God that he had found the true Shiloh, Ruler of Israel and Emmanuel. He was to pay a high price, however, as do all who follow Christ. His wife walked out on him; his parents disowned him. But he never gave up hope as he constantly prayed and reached out to his family. After 54 days, his wife joined him as a disciple of Jesus and, in time, his daughter also became a believer. But his son disowned him for many years until he was eventually reconciled both with his earthly and heavenly Father. In an extraordinary sequel some 18 months after he came to Christ, Max met up with Mrs Coulson, the mother of his dying young patient all those years earlier on the battlefield. With great joy, he was able to share how her son had set him on the path to a glorious future in Christ, which was to touch lives across the world, including my home county of Yorkshire in England. In fact, he came to live in Leeds to reach out to the Jewish community there and is buried at Lawnswood Cemetery in the city. An Irish friend of mine, Colin Nevin, has visited the grave, which includes an excerpt from one of the doctor’s hymns, I am Coming Soon, and was able to give a copy of Max’s story to a caretaker, so continuing the evangelist’s legacy more than a century after his death in 1892, aged 64. A 54-minute movie – Rossvally: From the Synagogue to the Saviour – has been produced on DVD and can apparently be ordered online. content: By Charles Gardner — We used to be regular viewers of the The Great British Bake-Off TV series, now being screened on Channel 4, celebrating the efforts of amateur contestants in the kitchen. My wife is qualified in home economics and once, in her far-off student days, helped Mary Berry out over the weekend. I too like to lend a hand with my cooking skills. So when, the other day, we were intrigued to see how new presenter Nigella Lawson was doing on the show, we switched it on – and were truly appalled at the foul language spewing out of the mouths of at least two contestants. Taking the name of the Lord Jesus Christ in vain, they loudly expressed their frustration (rather than praise) at things going wrong with their concoctions in front of more than seven million viewers. We switched it off, vowing to complain in the strongest possible terms, which I have since done. And though it’s hard to be surprised at the language regularly heard on television programmes these days, I was shocked to the core by Channel 4’s response, basically saying that this particularly offensive blasphemy doesn’t come under the category of “strong language”. Really? It’s surely the worst of them all. “We are sorry to hear you were offended by some of the language used within the programme,” they wrote. “Whilst we do appreciate that you find the use of such phrases or words unacceptable, we are not obliged under the Ofcom code to obscure them, nor do they fall under the category for strong language. We therefore have no obligation to bleep them either pre- or post-watershed.” I had suggested that they could at least have edited them out, adding that they were being very hypocritical as they wouldn’t have allowed swearing in the name of Mohammed, a point which they ignored. Have we sunk so low in our nation that there is nothing left that is sacred, except woke left-wing ideology and appeasement of those who hate the God of Israel and his Son Jesus, our Lord? But we have forsaken the God who brought peace and prosperity to Britain, and who saved us from Nazi invasion, for the idols of food and celebrity. Shame on us! Is it not time the Christian world woke up and stood against this flood of filth in our midst, which will sweep us away into the oblivion of a third-rate country if we do not act soon. Where has the ‘land of hope and glory’ gone? The ‘mother of the free’ we sing about at the Proms, calling on the God ‘who made thee mighty’ to ‘make thee mightier yet’? The Apostle Paul was surely prophesying the decline and fall of the Roman Empire in his letter to the early Christians in Rome (a mixture of Jews and Gentiles), when he wrote: “The wrath of God is being revealed from heaven against all the godlessness and wickedness of men who suppress the truth by their wickedness, since what may be known about God is plain to them, because God has made it plain to them. For since the creation of the world God’s invisible qualities – his eternal power and divine nature – have been clearly seen, being understood from what has been made, so that men are without excuse.” (Romans 1:18-20) The post Offended by foul language on food show first appeared on God Reports .

content: By Mike Shreve — Tent meeting in the 80s Evangelism has been my focus for 55 years, ministering throughout the United States and in 14 other nations. God mercifully saved me during the Jesus Revolution (1970), out of a hippie lifestyle and a passionate, though misguided pursuit of truth through far eastern religious practices (yoga and meditation). Shortly after encountering Jesus and being delivered, along with another brother in the Lord, I began hitchhiking around the country, preaching the Gospel on street corners and college campuses. That developed through the years into ministry in churches, auditoriums, conferences, and tent crusades. Supernatural provision and divine intervention has always carried me, through every phase of this five-and-a-half-decade-long adventure. However, the following story is a classic. For about 25 years I carried big Gospel tents around the country. At the time of this “miracle,” I was transporting a 60’ x 90’ tent from one city to the next in an old, dilapidated bus that kept introducing new challenges to our amateur mechanic skills (putting it mildly). One day, on our way to Tampa, Florida—unfortunately—we hit a large pothole in the road that put a serious dent in the rear left rim on which a large truck tire was mounted. From that point, the inner tube would not retain air, making it necessary to stop every thirty miles or so to fill it up again . . . and again . . . and again . . . making the trip painfully slow. Adding to the problem, the other rear tire was bald, and we had no spare (couldn’t afford one). So, a flat would have brought us to a complete standstill. Sometimes, I think back on those days (when our zeal for the Kingdom outran any wisdom we might have possessed), and I marvel at the many times God took care of us anyway (like the loving heavenly Father that He is). Thousands of pounds of equipment were packed into that groaning, creaking, rusty, decrepit bus — heavy canvas tent sections, metal poles, stakes, platform, and 300 chairs—and only a few days allowed in between cities for transit and setup. No, we really could not afford any setbacks. And yes, a lot of “faith prayers” were uttered during every trip (or were they “presumptive proclamations”—not sure—maybe a mix of the two). An old split rim tire mounted on an old bus Once we got to Tampa, attempting to be frugal, I visited the junkyards hoping to find a used replacement rim. As if they had conspired to dissuade me, every junkyard owner/manager shot down my hopes with a similar assessment, “Fella, you won’t find one of them old split-rims anywhere. They’re dangerous. When you try to mount a tire on one, they can snap open and injure somebody real bad, cutting off a hand, even killing a person. We melted ‘em all down as scrap metal.” (Go ahead, look them up online—they were even called “widow-makers.”) It was the same story everywhere I went. Nobody could help. Then three weeks passed and we had to pack the bus and head to our next location—Bessemer City, North Carolina. It was a college-level, biblically-sound course on developing long-suffering and patience: stopping every thirty miles or so to air up that unpredictable tire, pleading with God to somehow supernaturally assist us in our journey by making sure none of the tires blew. Somehow, we made it—around 600 miles—stopping about 25 times. Then an incredible miracle happened! God did it and I still feel awestruck, just writing about it. As we turned into the fairgrounds area, right in the middle of the entrance were two brand new, neatly-stacked truck tires (unclaimed), exactly the size we used on the bus—mounted (you guessed it!) on the very same split rims our bus required. Talk about worshiping God—we launched into a praise session right then and there! What were the odds? We all knew it had to be God.
